Article Title: US heatwave: Miami hits 100°F record as Oklahoma sizzles at 112°F
Article Text:
Ajogger pushes through the sweltering Miami heatwave, passing a sign holder seeking shade under an umbrella. (Photo: @elnuevoherald)​​​​​

Miami hit 100 degrees fahrenheit on Tuesday for only the second time in more than 130 years of records, tying its all-time high as a heat wave stretched from Texas to the Southeast.The city's only previous 100-degree reading was recorded on July 21, 1942. The latest record also fits into a broader trend of extreme warming linked to human-caused greenhouse gas emissions.Yet Miami's 100-degree record looks modest beside temperature extremes elsewhere in the US. Kingfisher, Oklahoma, reached 112 degrees on Tuesday, a record for August 18, while Oklahoma's all-time state high stands at 120 degrees and Minnesota's at 115. Florida's statewide record is 109 degrees, according to Cable News Network (CNN).Miami's relatively low record is largely a product of its coastal setting. The nearby ocean heats more slowly than land, while regular Atlantic sea breezes typically bring cooler marine air inland and help keep daytime temperatures from reaching the extremes more common in the country's dry interior.This moderating effect weakened on Tuesday, when west winds kept Miami's usual cooling sea breeze from developing along the coast.Drier regions can heat much more sharply, helping explain why the highest temperatures in the US are generally recorded in the desert Southwest rather than the humid Southeast.Miami's high humidity, however, means temperatures do not need to reach desert-like levels to become dangerous. Heat and moisture together can make it harder for the human body to cool itself, increasing the risk of heat-related illness.The city and much of the Southeast have also seen a sharp rise in extreme heat in recent decades. Miami now records 44 more above-normal summer days than it did in the 1970s, according to Climate Central, a US-based climate research group.Miami's average temperature during June, July and August has risen by 2.6 degrees fahrenheit. Climate Central also found that the annual number of days classified as dangerous humid heat — when the maximum wet-bulb temperature reaches at least 77°F — rose from an average of 50 in the 1970s to 117 during 2016-2025.The group estimated that human-caused climate change, largely driven by the burning of fossil fuels, accounted for about 80 of those 117 days.Miami's heat index, which accounts for the effect of humidity on how hot conditions feel, reached 107 degrees on Tuesday. A stalled heat dome, a persistent area of high pressure that traps hot air, drove the wider heat wave, which continued across much of the southern US on Wednesday.Heat advisories covered all of the Florida Peninsula on Wednesday except the Florida Keys, with Miami forecast to reach the mid-to-upper 90s as dangerous heat and humidity persisted.
Article Summary: Miami hit 100 degrees fahrenheit on Tuesday for only the second time in more than 130 years of records. The city's only previous 100-degree reading was recorded on July 21, 1942. The latest record fits into a broader trend of extreme warming linked to human-caused greenhouse gas emissions.

Article Title: 75,000 still without power in northwest Indiana, outages may last until Aug 25
Article Text:
A utility worker repairs overhead power lines from a bucket truck boom lift near a utility pole, while other laborers assess a damaged rooftop in the United States. (Photo: @theinformant_x)​​​​​

City grid needs extensive rebuilding

Generator costs, insulin storage add to strain

Utility rejects concerns Gary is being ignored

At least seven deaths reported since Aug 11

Power fails again at undamaged home

Eight days after severe storms swept through northwest Indiana, about 75,000 customers of Northern Indiana Public Service Co (NIPSCO) were still without power late Wednesday afternoon.More than 20,000 were in Gary, a city in northwest Indiana's Lake County, where full restoration is not expected until Aug 25, reported news agency Associated Press.Lake County, along the Illinois border, accounted for most of the remaining outages. As repair crews worked around the clock, residents returned to community centres in Gary for hot meals and to charge their phones.The outages date to severe weather that began on Aug 11 and initially knocked out service to about 300,000 NIPSCO customers. The utility has called it the largest and most widespread outage event in its history, the Associated Press reported.In Gary alone, roughly 300 poles and 44 transmission poles require repair or replacement, said Melody Birmingham, executive vice-president and group president, utilities, at NiSource, NIPSCO's parent company.Winds reached 159kmph at Gary/Chicago International Airport during the Aug 11 storm.The National Weather Service preliminarily confirmed the system as a derecho — a widespread, long-lived line of thunderstorms that causes significant wind damage.The agency said winds of roughly 113kmph to 161kmph swept across parts of eastern Illinois and northwest Indiana. Five tornadoes had also been confirmed in its initial assessment.Birmingham described the loss of perishable food and days without air conditioning as a “real burden” after what she called a “historic storm”. “These aren’t simple repairs,” Birmingham said at a news conference. “These are systems that are being rebuilt.”For some residents, the long wait for power has become expensive.Jeremy Spurrier, 51, said he was fortunate to have a generator at his Portage home, about 64km southwest of Chicago, but keeping it running costs about $75 a day. His family has largely switched to non-perishable food such as soup.The blackout has also complicated how Spurrier stores his insulin. He drives to Illinois for ice to keep it cold. “If I run out of ice, that’s several hundred dollars of insulin just ruined,” he said.In majority-Black Gary, some residents have complained that their community is being overlooked as the outage stretches into a second week.Birmingham, who is Black, rejected suggestions that lower-income residents were receiving less attention and blamed social-media posts for fuelling that perception. She said customers were also without power in areas that were probably affluent. “This has nothing to do with race or any type of division,” Birmingham said. “It’s really a matter of where the storm hit.”Gary Mayor Eddie Melton acknowledged the strain, describing residents as “frustrated and exhausted”, but said more than 600 linemen were working to restore electricity in the city.“I want to reiterate this is clearly not just a Gary situation. It is a northwest Indiana situation,” Melton said.That wider impact was reflected in outage figures from last week. Reuters reported that Indiana was the hardest-hit state in the Midwest, with more than 215,000 customers without electricity at one stage and NIPSCO accounting for about 199,000 of them.At least seven people had died since the storms began on Aug 11, including a 4-year-old boy, three men and three women, according to Liz Woods, a spokesperson for the Indiana Department of Homeland Security.Elsewhere in Indiana, rivers reached record levels and roads and bridges were damaged or washed out. More than 350 evacuations were carried out, along with scores of rescues and welfare checks.Myra Carden, 74, said the storm left her Whiting home untouched, “not even a chair was blown over in the yard” yet by Wednesday she was dealing with her second blackout.Carden lives with her son and three dogs. Their first outage lasted more than two days before power returned, only to fail again on Tuesday.She said she had reported the outage more than once but was repeatedly told that an earlier report had already been registered. “More than once I have put in an outage report,” she said. “All I get back is, ‘You already put in a report.’ Well, what do you want me to do? ... This doesn’t make sense. Of course I’m not a lineman; I’m a paralegal.”Carden runs a generator for the refrigerator only when someone is home to monitor it. She also has a garage freezer packed with beef and chicken and said she was sure all of it would have to be thrown away.For Gary, the Aug 25 estimate means some customers could remain without electricity for nearly two weeks after the Aug 11 storm. Reuters reported last week that NIPSCO had expected to restore about 90% of affected customers by Aug 18 and complete restoration systemwide by Aug 21, four days before Gary's current target.
Article Summary: About 75,000 customers of Northern Indiana Public Service Co (NIPSCO) were still without power late Wednesday afternoon. More than 20,000 were in Gary, a city in northwest Indiana's Lake County, where full restoration is not expected until Aug 25. At least seven people had died since the storms began on Aug 11.

Article Title: Pennsylvania crash: One killed in ‘violent’ collision between Cessna 150 and police helicopter
Article Text:
The midair collision occurred in Carlisle, Pennsylvania

The pilot of a Cessna 150 plane was killed when the aircraft collided with a Pennsylvania State Police Bell 407 helicopter near a runway at a small airport in Carlisle, Pennsylvania, authorities said.Both state troopers aboard the helicopter survived the collision on Wednesday evening (local time).According to Lt Col George Bivens, Pennsylvania's acting police commissioner, the Cessna 150 veered into the helicopter, which was near the ground."When I say it was a very violent crash, that plane was cut into a lot of pieces," Bivens told a news conference. He explained that investigators would also determine whether the pilot was the only person aboard the Cessna, a two-seat aircraft typically used for flight training."Both of the pilots in the Bell 407 were trapped until one pushed out a window and helped the other out through the window. The helicopter had been performing a training exercise," he added.The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) had earlier described the incident as a midair collision, although Bivens did not clarify whether the plane was off the ground.Officials are withholding the identity of the person who died until the next of kin are notified.Photos and videos posted on social media showed the helicopter lying on its side near aircraft debris in a field, with a line of emergency vehicles nearby.The FAA and NTSB are investigating the crash.Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy noted that he had been in touch with the governor.
Article Summary: The pilot of a Cessna 150 plane was killed when the aircraft collided with a Pennsylvania State Police Bell 407 helicopter. Both state troopers aboard the helicopter survived the collision on Wednesday evening (local time) The FAA and NTSB are investigating the crash.

Article Title: Meet Audrey Zheng, the 17-year-old Pennsylvania student who developed a pancreatic cancer test; it correctly identified 87% of patients and 87.5% without the disease
Article Text:
Audrey Zheng (North Allegheny Senior High School, Pittsburgh, PA)

Targeting microscopic messages in blood

Tracking genetic mutations for diagnostic precision

Leadership across science and community service

A 17-year-old student from Pennsylvania has developed an innovative bioengineering method to detect early-stage pancreatic cancer from blood samples, tackling one of the biggest challenges in cancer diagnosis. Audrey Zheng, a senior at North Allegheny Senior High School in Wexford, developed a technique that uses tiny magnetic beads to capture tumor-derived particles moving through the bloodstream. In clinical testing, her method correctly identified 87 per cent of patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and correctly ruled out the disease in 87.5 per cent of people who did not have it. Her research earned her a place as a national finalist in the 2026 Regeneron Science Talent Search, one of the leading science and mathematics competitions for high school seniors, run by the Society for Science.Pancreatic cancer is difficult to detect because it often causes no clear symptoms in its early stages. By the time symptoms such as abdominal pain or jaundice appear, the cancer may have already spread to nearby organs, making surgery much harder or impossible. Current screening methods, including standard imaging and general protein biomarkers, often cannot detect small, localized tumors. Zheng focused on extracellular vesicles, tiny membrane-covered sacs that are constantly released by human cells into the blood.These biological packages carry molecular material, including proteins and genetic information, that can reveal the condition of the cells they came from. To separate cancer-related vesicles from the trillions of healthy vesicles in a blood sample, Zheng created a mixture of magnetic nanospheres coated with three specific antibodies. These antibodies were designed to attach to cancer-related surface molecules found on tumor-derived vesicles. After the antibodies attach to the cancer vesicles, a magnetic field pulls the nanosphere-bound particles out of the blood sample. This physically separates the targeted particles from healthy biological material.After isolating the targeted extracellular vesicles, Zheng extracted and examined the genetic material inside them. She focused on mutations in the KRAS gene, a major cancer-driving mutation found in more than 90 per cent of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma cases. By testing the DNA inside the isolated vesicles for these mutations, the diagnostic system used two layers of confirmation. First, it identified vesicles using their cancer-related surface markers. Then, it checked their genetic material for cancer-causing mutations. This two-step approach helped the test achieve strong sensitivity and specificity. In comparative testing, the method correctly identified 87 per cent of confirmed cancer cases while keeping the false-positive rate at 12.5 per cent. Early detection is especially important for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, where five-year survival remains below 13 per cent, largely because the disease is often found late. Detecting the cancer at Stage I or II, when the tumor may still be removed through surgery, can greatly improve the chances of long-term survival.The daughter of Ming Ni and Siyang Zheng, Audrey Zheng balances her bioengineering research with leadership roles at North Allegheny High School. She serves as co-president of the math and physics club and captain of the school's tennis team. Her interest in practical engineering also extends to community service. Zheng founded and serves as president of The Food Lounge Pittsburgh, a non-profit organisation that has organised more than 50 volunteer events supporting regional food banks and community kitchens. Building on her work with magnetic nanoparticles, Zheng is now adapting her nanosphere technology to develop a separate portable sensor that could quickly detect common food allergens in field settings. Her pancreatic cancer diagnostic project was presented at the Society for Science Public Day exhibition in Washington, D.C., where 40 Regeneron Science Talent Search finalists showcased their research to scientific panels and the public.
Article Summary: Audrey Zheng, a senior at North Allegheny Senior High School in Wexford, developed a technique that uses tiny magnetic beads to capture tumor-derived particles moving through the bloodstream. In clinical testing, her method correctly identified 87 per cent of patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma and correctly ruled out the disease in 87.5 per cent.

Article Title: FBI puts Indian national Major Singh on Most Wanted list
Article Text:
​Major Singh added to FBI's Most Wanted list/Image: FBI

Indian national Major Singh, described by the Federal Bureau of Investigation as a key operative of the Jaggu Bhagwanpuria gang, has been added to the FBI’s Most Wanted list over his alleged involvement in the gang's activities in America.Singh, 29, faces federal charges in the Central District of California over an alleged conspiracy to violate the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations (RICO) Act and a conspiracy involving the unlicensed trade of firearms.A federal arrest warrant was issued for Singh on June 25, 2026. The FBI is seeking information that could lead to his arrest.The agency describes the Jaggu Bhagwanpuria gang as a transnational organised crime group that originated in Punjab and operates in California and elsewhere in the US.The FBI alleges that the group is involved in racketeering, illegal firearms trafficking and the distribution of controlled substances.The agency has asked anyone with information about Singh to contact its nearest office, a US embassy or consulate, or submit information through its online tip system.The development comes after a major international crackdown on India-linked organised crime groups.Earlier this month, authorities in the US, Canada and Europe arrested 24 people, including 11 in California, in a joint operation targeting three India-based transnational crime groups.The US Department of Justice has charged 37 people in the wider investigation, including jailed Punjab gangsters Lawrence Bishnoi and Jaggu Bhagwanpuria, as part of Operation Hardball.
Article Summary: Major Singh is a key operative of the Jaggu Bhagwanpuria gang. The 29-year-old faces federal charges in the Central District of California. The FBI is seeking information that could lead to his arrest. The development comes after a major international crackdown on India-linked crime groups.

Article Title: ‘All trade, commercial exchanges halted’: How UAE responded to Iran’s latest ballistic missile attack
Article Text:
A view of the Dubai city skyline. (AP Photo)

UAE freezes economic ties with Tehran

Iran denies launching missiles

Missile attack threatens fragile UAE-Iran thaw

Strait of Hormuz tensions add to pressure

Trump tensions with Oman over Iran deal

Iran says Strait will not reopen yet

Poll Vote & Share your view How concerned are you about the impact of military actions in the Gulf region on global trade? Very concerned Somewhat concerned Not concerned Indifferent 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

The United Arab Emirates has suspended all trade, commercial exchanges and financial transactions with Iran after accusing Tehran of launching two ballistic missiles towards the Gulf state, dealing a fresh blow to efforts to ease tensions between the two countries.The UAE defence ministry said its air-defence systems detected two ballistic missiles launched from Iran towards its territory on Tuesday. The incident triggered an emergency alert on residents' phones and was described as the first direct Iranian attack on the UAE since May.The ministry later said its assessment indicated that the missiles had been targeting maritime traffic. One missile fell into the sea outside the UAE's territorial waters, while the other fell within them. No damage or injuries were reported.Following the missile incident, the UAE foreign affairs ministry announced that it was halting economic engagement with Iran until further notice.The ministry said that “in light of regional escalations that undermine regional and international peace and security, all trade, commercial exchanges, and financial transactions with Iran have been halted until further notice”.The decision threatens to reverse a gradual restoration of economic and diplomatic links between Abu Dhabi and Tehran. Trade between the UAE and Iranian ports had resumed in some areas, while certain Iranian flights to the UAE had also quietly returned.The emergency alert issued on Tuesday was the first such warning in several months, apart from a false alert in June. Dubai's financial district had also begun filling up with bankers, while Emirati authorities had started allowing some 20,000 Iranian residents who were outside the country when the war began to return to the UAE.Iran has denied the UAE's accusation, with Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei rejecting the claim and warning that such allegations could undermine regional efforts to rebuild trust.Baghaei “completely rejected” the UAE's claim and expressed regret over the accusations against Iran, according to a statement issued by the Iranian Foreign Ministry.“This behaviour is contrary to the principle of good neighbourliness and disrupts ongoing efforts to strengthen trust between regional countries and prevent the escalation of insecurity in the region,” Baghaei said.The Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson also called on regional countries to refrain from making “baseless accusations” against Tehran.“The Foreign Ministry spokesman called on all regional parties to refrain from making baseless accusations against the Islamic Republic of Iran, considering the existing complexities due to the ongoing evils of the US and the Zionist regime against regional peace and security, especially the history of numerous false flag operations,” he said.The UAE defence ministry, meanwhile, maintained that its air-defence systems had detected the missiles.“The first fell outside the country's territorial waters, while the second fell within its territorial waters,” the UAE Ministry of Defence said in a post on X.The UAE military said its forces remained on high alert and were prepared to respond to threats against the country's security and sovereignty.The latest confrontation comes after more than two months of efforts by Abu Dhabi and Tehran to reduce tensions that had escalated following the US and Israeli war against Iran that began on February 28.During the conflict, Iran launched repeated missile and drone attacks against neighbouring Gulf states, including the UAE, accusing them of enabling US and Israeli military operations.The UAE was among the Gulf states most heavily targeted, sustaining almost 3,000 missile and drone attacks. Abu Dhabi also carried out scores of strikes against Iran, taking a more hawkish position towards Tehran than several of its Gulf neighbours.Tensions later eased after Washington and Tehran reached a memorandum of understanding in June. However, the agreement began to unravel in early July, after which Iran shifted much of its military focus towards Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan.In recent months, the UAE had sought to rebuild diplomatic and economic channels with Iran while maintaining close military ties with Israel and the United States. Emirati officials have repeatedly said they want to avoid being drawn further into a wider regional conflict.That balancing act is now under growing pressure following the latest missile incident.The confrontation also comes amid escalating tensions around the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial route for global oil and natural gas shipments.The UAE accused Iran earlier this month of attacking ships operated by Abu Dhabi National Oil Company in the strategic waterway. Tehran has also maintained restrictions on traffic through the strait while issuing increasingly aggressive military rhetoric.A separate maritime incident was reported on Tuesday when an unidentified projectile struck a ship as it sailed out of the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Oman. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations centre said the strike damaged the vessel's engine room and caused a casualty, while the Omani Coast Guard assisted other crew members.Another cargo vessel was struck by multiple projectiles about 40 nautical miles, or 74 kilometres, southeast of Mokha in Yemen and was declared a “constructive total loss”, according to the British maritime monitoring agency. The agency did not identify the projectiles or those responsible.The incidents have added to concerns over the safety of commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Red Sea region, both vital routes for global trade.The maritime crisis has also drawn Oman into a dispute between Washington and Tehran over arrangements for shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.US President Donald Trump threatened Oman after becoming dissatisfied with an emerging agreement between Muscat and Tehran aimed at managing ship traffic through the strategic waterway, according to two regional officials cited by The Associated Press.The officials said the Trump administration objected to parts of the proposed agreement, including joint Iranian and Omani management of the exit route from the strait and voluntary fees on vessels linked to security and maritime environmental protection.Trump on Monday threatened to bomb Oman as it worked with Iran on an agreement intended to reopen the strait and potentially allow Washington and Tehran to resume negotiations aimed at ending the conflict.He later posted a map on social media depicting the Strait of Hormuz as US territory. Trump had previously floated the idea during an Oval Office exchange, saying, “I like the idea of declaring it a territory,” without providing further details.The White House referred to Trump's earlier Oval Office remarks when asked about the latest comments and declined to provide additional details.Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi responded to Trump's remarks on social media.“Just as Trump correctly wrote the name of the eternal Persian Gulf, his delusion regarding the Strait of Hormuz will soon either be corrected, or we will correct this deluded man’s delusions for him,” Gharibabadi wrote on X.Trump has previously threatened Oman over its dealings with Iran. In May, he told reporters during a Cabinet meeting that Oman “will behave just like everybody else, or we will have to blow them up.”Iran has maintained that the Strait of Hormuz will not fully reopen until Washington meets its conditions, including commitments related to sanctions, frozen assets and military operations.“Until the United States fulfills its commitments under the agreement, including lifting the blockade, releasing frozen assets, lifting oil sanctions, ending threats and military operations on all fronts, and implementing the other conditions to which it committed, the Strait of Hormuz will not reopen,” Iranian parliamentary speaker and former US-Iran negotiator Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf said.Trump, however, said on Tuesday that the United States had no planned talks with Iran and insisted that the strait was “open and operating”, despite limited maritime traffic and reports of fresh attacks.He also said the US blockade of the waterway remained “in full force and effect” and claimed that all water mines had been removed.Egypt has backed the Iranian-Omani negotiations, saying an agreement could help create conditions for Washington and Tehran to return to talks.The Egyptian foreign ministry said the agreement could pave the way for a “comprehensive and permanent deal that addresses all concerns and enhances regional security and stability."The latest developments leave the UAE facing renewed security pressure as its decision to suspend economic ties with Iran threatens to derail a fragile diplomatic thaw, while tensions around the Strait of Hormuz and wider regional military activity continue to intensify.
Article Summary: UAE accuses Tehran of launching two ballistic missiles towards the Gulf state. The incident triggered an emergency alert on residents' phones. The UAE foreign affairs ministry announced that it was halting economic engagement with Iran until further notice. Iran has denied the UAE's accusation, with Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei warning such allegations could undermine regional efforts to rebuild trust.

Article Title: Indonesian woman gives birth under torchlight during magnitude 7.7 earthquake
Article Text:
Maria Florida Nogo Kelen gave birth by torchlight during Indonesia’s 7.7 earthquake, naming baby Gempita/Image: Reuters

gempa

A 39-year-old woman gave birth by emergency caesarean section under torchlight after a magnitude-7.7 earthquake cut power to a hospital in eastern Indonesia.Maria Florida Nogo Kelen was eight months pregnant when the earthquake struck East Nusa Tenggara on Saturday. Her complicated pregnancy meant delaying the delivery could have triggered a potentially fatal seizure.Doctors performed the surgery as aftershocks continued and parts of the hospital were damaged.“During the surgery, I was not afraid,” Kelen told Reuters. “I had to be healthy for my kids.”Her obstetrician, Yona Sara Pardede, said the medical team had little choice but to proceed despite the conditions.“As humans we were afraid. The surgery was difficult as she was a small baby. I ask God, please help us. We don't even have a ventilator,” Pardede said.The baby girl was born weighing 1.3kg during the aftershocks. Her mother named her Gempita, derived from, the Indonesian word for earthquake.The premature baby has remained stable in an incubator placed on grass inside a tent in Nagekeo. Kelen suffered a haemorrhage after giving birth but survived.“I was very grateful for the doctors, even when the room had collapsed, they did not abandon us,” she said.The earthquake caused widespread damage across the province. Medical teams have been treating patients in tents outside damaged hospitals, while rescuers have been searching buildings for people trapped beneath rubble.At least 995 aftershocks have been recorded since Saturday, although only 46 were felt. A magnitude-5.9 tremor struck on Monday.The earthquake hit shortly before 6 am at a depth of about 10km, with its epicentre around 68km northwest of Ende on Flores, according to the US Geological Survey.Tsunami warnings were issued after the quake but were later lifted after no significant sea-level changes were recorded.The disaster has killed at least 68 people, injured 135 and damaged more than 1,300 homes, including nearly 250 that were destroyed on Flores. About 5,000 people have moved into temporary shelters, while the provincial governor has declared a 14-day state of emergency.
Article Summary: Maria Florida Nogo Kelen was eight months pregnant when the earthquake struck East Nusa Tenggara on Saturday. Her complicated pregnancy meant delaying the delivery could have triggered a potentially fatal seizure. Doctors performed the surgery as aftershocks continued and parts of the hospital were damaged.

Article Title: Imran Khan’s sister meets him after 9 months as Pakistan SC orders hospital transfer for jailed ex-PM
Article Text:
Former Pak PM is set to be shifted to a hospital after top court's order over health concerns

Former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan ’s sister Noreen Niazi met him at Rawalpindi's Adiala Jail on Tuesday after a gap of around nine months, following a Supreme Court order allowing weekly meetings between the former prime minister and his family amid concerns over his health.The meeting lasted around 15 minutes, according to jail sources, cited by Express Tribune. Noreen briefed Imran on the Supreme Court’s order regarding his transfer to Islamabad’s Shifa International Hospital and enquired about his health. The two also discussed ongoing legal matters.Noreen confirmed after the meeting that she had met her brother but did not speak to the media, in line with an assurance given before the court. She later left Adiala Jail with her sisters Aleema Khan and Uzma Khan.Imran also met his wife, Bushra Bibi, with their meeting lasting around 30-35 minutes. Bushra earlier met her daughter, Mubashra Sheikh, and sister-in-law Mehrunnisa.Before entering the jail, Noreen told reporters that she would inform Imran that “the Supreme Court has granted you permission” to meet his family. She also said she would brief him about efforts made by PTI workers on his behalf.The meetings followed a three-member Supreme Court bench headed by Justice Shahid Waheed directing the government to facilitate weekly meetings between Imran and his family. The court was hearing petitions concerning his access to his sisters and personal physicians, as well as his medical condition.The order came after a medical board report and a report by the Adiala Jail superintendent were submitted to the court. The reports recommended more frequent meetings with Imran’s immediate family and spouse to help manage his blood pressure and anxiety.The Supreme Court also ordered that Imran be moved to Shifa International Hospital for treatment and directed the formation of a medical board comprising an eye specialist, general physician, cardiologist and his personal physician, Dr Faisal Sultan. Dr Uzma was also to be included in the board.The court ordered that his medical records remain confidential and barred political activity or media interactions outside the hospital. It also directed authorities to arrange telephone contact between Imran and his children.Justice Waheed stressed that access to family could not be treated as a favour, describing the meetings as a fundamental right rather than a concession. The court, however, required PTI representatives to refrain from political activity or media engagement after meeting Imran, a condition the party said it would follow.Aleema Khan welcomed the order, saying the family had been demanding hospital treatment for Imran for months. Speaking to reporters at the Dahgal checkpoint in Rawalpindi, she said she was happy about the meeting but remained uncertain about whether the development signalled a broader change in circumstances.“"Words cannot describe how happy I am about the meeting. I cannot even imagine where I would have got sweets from. I have appeared before the ATC Rawalpindi from the Supreme Court,” Aleema said.She also rejected suggestions that the family was politicising Imran’s health, saying they were speaking as his sisters.PTI spokesperson Niazullah Khan Niazi said Imran had a right to meet his family twice a week but that authorities had continued to restrict access despite an Islamabad High Court order. He said the party would comply with the Supreme Court’s direction against political statements after meetings.Concerns over Imran’s health have intensified in recent months. A medical report submitted to the Supreme Court said he had experienced fluctuating blood pressure, palpitations, headaches, restlessness and significant anxiety.A PIMS cardiologist who examined him on August 1 recorded his blood pressure at 140/100mmHg and recommended measures to reduce mental stress, including more frequent meetings with his wife and access to reading material. A four-member medical board that examined him on August 10 recorded his blood pressure at 140/80mmHg and recommended walking, relaxation and more frequent interaction with his immediate family and spouse.The report said Imran had undergone at least 39 medical check-ups since his incarceration, with jail medical officers examining him three times a day. It also said his ECG was normal and his vision had improved to almost normal following treatment for an eye condition.PTI has questioned the authenticity and completeness of the medical documentation and demanded examinations by Imran’s personal physicians, Dr Asim Yusuf and Dr Faisal Sultan, as well as an independent medical board. The government has rejected claims that he is being denied proper medical care, saying he is receiving treatment from specialists in accordance with the law and court orders.A report submitted to the Supreme Court in February had said Imran’s right eye was functioning at only 15% capacity. The court subsequently ordered that he be granted access to his personal physicians in Adiala Jail.Imran and Bushra Bibi remain incarcerated at Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi. They were sentenced in December 2025 to 17 years in prison in the Toshakhana-II case over allegations that they unlawfully retained a Bulgari jewellery set gifted by the Saudi crown prince.Imran has been in custody since August 2023, initially following his conviction in the £190 million corruption case. He also faces pending trials under Pakistan’s Anti-Terrorism Act in connection with the May 9, 2023, protests.Imran, who served as prime minister from 2018 until his ouster through a parliamentary no-confidence vote in 2022, and his supporters have consistently maintained that the cases against him are politically motivated and aimed at preventing his political comeback.
Article Summary: Imran's sister Noreen Niazi met him at Rawalpindi's Adiala Jail on Tuesday after a gap of around nine months. Meeting followed a Supreme Court order allowing weekly meetings between the former prime minister and his family amid concerns over his health.

Article Title: Iran claims control, ships choose Omani route: What’s changing in Strait of Hormuz
Article Text:
80% of ships take Omani route as Iran’s grip weakens

Shipping traffic slows amid uncertainty

How the US-Iran conflict unfolded

US claims control as Oman-Iran talks continue

The battle for control of the Strait of Hormuz has emerged as a key focus of the Iran war, with both Iran and the United States claiming the upper hand in recent months. The competing claims have created uncertainty over the extent of control exercised by either side over the critical waterway.However, shipping data indicates that the United States is gaining ground as its navy patrols the strait, while Iran appears to be losing control over parts of the waterway.More than 80% of vessel that have transited through the Strait of Hormuz over the past two weeks have used the Omani route, a UN-authorised shipping channel opposed by Iran, according to Kpler, which tracks vessels using transponders and satellite data cited by CNN.Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz slowed on Tuesday, with preliminary data showing most shipowners continued to avoid the key waterway amid a lack of clear signals on its reopening, Reuters reported.Iran, which has declared the Strait of Hormuz under its control, has attacked dozens of ships attempting to transit the waterway along Oman’s northern coast.Despite the risks, most vessels have recently continued to cross the strait, disregarding Iran’s demands and relying on protection from US naval forces.The expiration of the US-Iran Memorandum of Understanding this week has, in theory, allowed Iran to resume charging tolls on vessels using the Strait of Hormuz. However, Kpler data suggests that Iran has not been able to do so.The current traffic pattern marks a sharp contrast with a month ago, when Kpler recorded virtually no shipping activity along the Omani route. The steep decline in traffic along Iran’s preferred route has also prevented Tehran from collecting tolls on vessels passing through the strait, as it did in the spring.Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have chartered Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs), the largest oil tankers, to transport crude out of the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz. The oil is then transferred to customers’ tankers outside the danger zone in the Gulf of Oman, according to Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates.To avoid Iranian attacks, the tankers have switched off their transponders, sometimes for weeks at a time. Such “dark traffic” can evade some tracking services, including Kpler, although some vessels can still be detected through satellite data.The United States, however, has deployed significant military forces in the waterway and has reported substantially higher oil-shipping volumes than earlier estimates from traditional tracking services.US President Donald Trump said Monday that the United States had “total control over the strait”, a claim he has repeatedly made during the conflict. However, continued Iranian attacks and oil flows remaining well below pre-war levels suggest that the US does not have full control of the Strait of Hormuz.At the same time, if tankers are moving as much oil through the strait as the United States claims, Iran’s ability to deter shipping and maintain control of the waterway has weakened compared with a month or two ago.Meanwhile, Oman and Iran are holding talks to restore freedom of navigation through the strait without US involvement. The discussions could affect oil traffic and control of the strategic waterway, though their impact remains unclear.
Article Summary: More than 80% of vessel that have transited through the Strait of Hormuz over the past two weeks have used the Omani route. The steep decline in traffic along Iran’s preferred route has also prevented Tehran from collecting tolls on vessels passing through the strait.

Article Title: 'I don't have courage to take another loan': Indian student in Canada says going back home seems easier, sets up fundraiser
Article Text:
Indian student in Canada Samir Garhwal sets up a fundraiser to pay off his education loans as he was denied a work permit after completing his degree from Portage College.

Row over Portage College degrees

Samir Garhwal, an Indian student who got his degree from Canada's controversial Portage College, said he is in a worse situation now after completing his course than he was two years ago when he came to a new country with an education loan to repay. As thousands of Portage College students were denied work permits in Canada, they have two options left in front of them: going back to India or legally challenging the IRCC's decision to deny them work permits.In an interview with CityNews, Samir said he and his peers were relaxed after their course and were waiting for their work permits to come so that they could start working in Canada and gain Canadian experience. But there was a mass rejection of work permits, leading to the students protesting against the college and Canadian immigration. But as of now, there has been no solution.Canada identified some courses as eligible for a work permit and some as ineligible. There was a change of rule in 2024 that made many courses of this particular college ineligible, but these students enroled in the courses before that date in 2024 and were in the dark about their future in Canada for the last two years."I already took an education loan in India, and in my current situation, I am not willing to or don't have the courage to get another loan," Garhwal, who said he was working while studying in Canada, confessed.For Garhwal and many others, going back to India is the only plausible option as the legal option involves more money. Garhwal has set up a fundraiser to pay his education loan. "Three years ago, I moved to Canada with the hope of building a better future through education and hard work. I have worked toward my studies while managing the challenges of living in a new country, including tuition, living expenses, and other essential costs," Garhwal wrote in the fundraiser.Portage College said they were still seeking clarification on the denial of the work permits for its students. “We are continuing to seek clarification on the Post Graduation Work Permit issue. As each day goes by, we understand the uncertainty that grows for many of our affected graduates as we endeavour to clarify factual and sourced details. We remain committed to informing the public about new developments to the issue,” said Portage College Vice President Academics and Research Dr Donna Feledichuk. “We also encourage affected graduates to seek professional advice from certified immigration specialists.”Juno News reported that the Canadian Institute of Osteopathic Therapy (CIOT) in Calgary, the private college that partnered with Portage College, has two directors tied to a Punjabi recruitment firm whose director was arrested in India during a 2013 police investigation into alleged student immigration fraud.
Article Summary: Thousands of Portage College students were denied work permits in Canada. They have two options left in front of them: going back to India or legally challenging the IRCC's decision to deny them work permits. Samir Garhwal, an Indian student who got his degree from Canada's controversial college, said he is in a worse situation now after completing his course.

Article Title: In 1942, a US soldier wrote 300 love letters to his wife; 80 years later the mysterious box appeared at a USO office
Article Text:
This image layers a handwritten letter from 'Speedy' over a D-Day landing image, reflecting the personal and historical threads in the USO archive. Image Credit: Ryan LaBee/USO archival material and a public domain D-Day image

Who was Speedy Weber who wrote 300 love letters to his wife

A handwritten August 1942 letter from Louis Weber to his wife, Frances. Image Credit: USO

What made the mysterious box of letters so unique

Speedy wrote this June 1942 postcard to his wife, Frances. Image Credit: USO​

How did the letters reveal Speedy’s personality

What did Speedy write about the war in those letters

How were Speedy’s relatives finally found

What happened to Speedy and Frances after the war

Why do these letters matter today

In 2022, a cardboard box containing more than 300 letters written by a US Army soldier during the Second World War arrived unexpectedly at a United Service Organisations (USO) office in New York. The letters belonged to Louis ‘Speedy’ Weber, a young soldier who spent years overseas writing to his wife, Frances, while she remained at home in the Bronx. For decades, the couple’s story had remained largely private, but the discovery gave historians an unusually intimate view of an ordinary serviceman’s wartime life. As Smithsonian magazine reported, the letters eventually reached USO headquarters in Virginia, where archivist and historian Michael Case became determined to learn who Speedy was and what happened to the couple after the war. His search led to relatives who could finally put a face and family story to the name and his letters again.Louis Weber, better known as ‘Speedy,’ was just 23 when he entered the US Army in 1942. He had been married to Frances for only about a year when military service separated them. While he learned the routines of Army life, Frances remained in the Bronx, and letters became the couple’s main way of staying connected. As per Smithsonian magazine, Speedy wrote hundreds of letters during his years overseas.His correspondence came from places including Sicily, England, France, Belgium, Germany, Czechoslovakia and North Africa.The letters revealed a young man who was far more expressive than his ordinary circumstances might suggest. Smithsonian described his writing as ‘everyday elegant,’ noting that he used simple language while capturing the emotions of the moment. Speedy also had a playful side. He gave Frances a collection of affectionate nicknames, including ‘Dearest,’ ‘Legs,’ ‘Darling,’ ‘Knucklehead,’ ‘Shape’ and ‘Meatball. ’ Many letters ended with the same warm message, ‘You are always in my heart.’The USO receives many historical donations, but Speedy’s collection immediately stood apart. Michael Case was accustomed to seeing individual photographs, postcards, military pins and other small objects arriving at the organisation. More than 300 personal letters, however, offered something much more intimate. Case said reading the correspondence made him feel as though he was getting to know Speedy himself. The soldier was not a famous commander or public figure. He was simply a young man doing his job, missing his wife, making mistakes and trying to cope with a long separation. The mystery was that nobody knew who had donated the box. The letters eventually moved from the New York USO office to the organisation’s headquarters in Virginia. Researchers began trying to discover what had happened to Speedy and Frances after the war, but their initial efforts produced few answers.Speedy’s writing was often funny, affectionate and unexpectedly dramatic. In one 1942 letter, he joked that Frances could send herself to him by wrapping herself in a package marked ‘fragile.’ Yet the humour was often mixed with loneliness. In another letter, he looked ahead to the day when the war would end and imagined the couple taking a second honeymoon. He promised that it would be even better than their first. Then his mood changed. He wrote about how the couple were merely existing rather than truly living while they remained apart. He also asked Frances to remember the happiest times they had shared. The letters therefore became more than romantic messages. They recorded the emotional strain of wartime separation in the words of someone experiencing it himself.The correspondence also provided glimpses of major events in the Second World War. Speedy was in Europe around the time of D-Day and later described crossing the English Channel. In a June 1944 letter, he wrote about seeing ships stretching across the water and aircraft filling the sky. For him, it was a breathtaking sight that he said he would never forget. His letters also contained ordinary military frustrations. In early 1945, he told Frances that he had been reduced in rank from private first class to private. He joked that, whatever the reason, there was at least nowhere lower for him to go because private was the lowest rank. These small details helped historians see the war not only through major battles and official records, but through the everyday thoughts of an ordinary soldier.The search continued for years. In 2024, the USO worked with the Washington Post to investigate the mystery. Researchers established that Speedy and Frances had lived near each other in New York in 1940, but the investigation did not immediately produce anyone who knew them. The breakthrough came after amateur genealogist Matthew Brown began investigating the family. According to Smithsonian magazine, Brown searched and identified a possible relative named Arthur Serota. Serota, who lived in Los Angeles, knew nothing about the letters but knew Speedy well. He was Speedy’s nephew and remembered his uncle as a warm and generous man. Another relative, Karen Weber Figilis, also remembered Speedy and Frances from family gatherings. She had something particularly valuable, ‘two black-and-white photographs.’ One showed Speedy and Frances together, while another showed Speedy alone. For Case, the photographs finally put a face to the soldier whose words he had been reading.The letters showed only part of the couple’s life. After the war, Speedy returned home and worked as a truck driver, while Frances became a manager at the US Post Office. The couple never had children, but they remained together for the rest of their lives and eventually moved to Florida. Speedy died at 78 and Frances at 87, and they were buried together at a Jewish cemetery. Even after relatives were found, some questions remained. Only two of Frances’ letters survive in the collection, although Speedy’s writing suggests that she corresponded with him regularly. Nobody has established who carried the box of letters into the USO office in 2022. Case believes the collection may have been discovered while someone was clearing out a home, possibly after the owner’s death. Some letters were written on USO stationery, which may explain why someone chose to bring them to the organisation.Speedy Weber never set out to become a historical figure. He was simply writing to his wife during an difficult period of his life. That is precisely what makes the collection so valuable. As Smithsonian magazine noted, personal letters can show what major historical events felt like for ordinary people. Speedy’s correspondence captures homesickness, humour, frustration, affection and uncertainty in a way that formal military records rarely can. The mysterious box therefore preserved more than 300 pieces of a private love story. It also preserved the voice of an everyday American soldier who happened to witness some of the biggest moments of the Second World War. More than eight decades later, Speedy’s words have found new readers, while the mystery of who delivered the letters remains unsolved.
Article Summary: Louis 'Speedy' Weber was a young soldier who spent years overseas writing to his wife, Frances, while she remained at home in the Bronx. For decades, the couple's story had remained largely private, but the discovery gave historians an unusually intimate view of an ordinary serviceman’s wartime life.

Article Title: US debt tops $40 trillion - $20 trillion since Trump first took office
Article Text:
US debt hits record $40.047 trillion. Photo credit: AP

The US national debt has crossed the $40 trillion mark for the first time, according to Treasury data showed on Wednesday. The milestone comes as rising spending on defence, Social Security and Medicare, alongside mounting interest payments, pushes federal borrowing to a record level.The latest milestone comes as the pace of borrowing outstrips earlier forecasts, with longer-term obligations for healthcare and retirement benefits continuing to grow.The debt stood at $40.047 trillion on Tuesday, including $32.266 trillion held by the public and $7.782 trillion in intragovernmental holdings, according to Treasury data.This came less than five months after the debt crossed $39 trillion. It has more than doubled from $19.95 trillion when Donald Trump first took office in January 2017.Kush Desai, a White House spokesman, told AP that the Trump administration “has been focused on slashing waste, fraud, and abuse in federal spending while accelerating economic growth to get America’s debt-to-GDP ratio trending in the right direction.”According to news agency Reuters, the US budget deficit in the first 10 months of fiscal 2026 has already surpassed the full-year deficit recorded in fiscal 2025, with two months still remaining in the current fiscal year.But fiscal watchdogs warned that rising interest costs and spending on programmes including Social Security and Medicare are putting increasing pressure on the federal budget.“Forty trillion dollars of debt doesn’t exist solely on the government’s ledgers; it is felt throughout the economy and finds its way to the pocketbooks of people one way or another,” Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget told Reuters.Additionally, Trump’s second-term legislation, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, is expected to add another $4.7 trillion to the US debt, according to the Congressional Budget Office, the nonpartisan fiscal agency that provides budget analysis to Congress.The debt has risen sharply across successive administrations, with pandemic spending under Trump and former president Joe Biden accounting for a substantial portion of the increase. Public debt rose by $7.8 trillion during Trump’s first term and by $8.4 trillion during Biden’s presidency, according to the figures cited by Reuters.Interest costs have also become a major budget burden. In the first 10 months of fiscal 2026, interest payments surpassed Medicare spending to become the second-largest federal expenditure after Social Security.The Bipartisan policy center estimates that the US could reach its $41.1 trillion debt limit between late winter and mid-summer 2027, potentially forcing Congress to revisit the borrowing cap.
Article Summary: The US national debt has crossed the $40 trillion mark for the first time, according to Treasury data. The milestone comes as rising spending on defence, Social Security and Medicare, alongside mounting interest payments, pushes federal borrowing to a record level. The pace of borrowing outstrips earlier forecasts.

Article Title: In 1950, US former president Eisenhower bought a 189-acre Gettysburg farm for retirement. 17 years later, he gave the property to the nation
Article Text:
Ex- US President Eisenhower's early years at Gettysburg

Eisenhower purchased a 189-acre Gettysburg farm before becoming president

The house was rebuilt while he was president

Gettysburg became a working presidential retreat

Life after the presidency was quieter, but not inactive

The farm became part of their legacy

Eisenhower donated his Gettysburg farm after nearly two decades as his home

Gettysburg entered Dwight D. Eisenhower's life long before he became a general or president. In 1915, he arrived there as a West Point cadet, studying the ground where the Civil War's most famous battle had unfolded. Three years later, he was back, now a young Army officer assigned to Camp Colt, a tank training centre established on the battlefield. He had wanted to go overseas during the First World War, but his orders kept him in Pennsylvania, where he worked with soldiers preparing for deployment.Years passed, and Eisenhower's career carried him through senior military commands, the Second World War and eventually the White House. Yet Gettysburg remained familiar. As reported by the National Park Service (NPS), in 1950, he and Mamie bought a 189-acre farm beside the battlefield. It would eventually become their retirement home and the place where Eisenhower spent his final years.Eisenhower's relationship with Gettysburg began in the spring of 1915, when he was still a cadet at the US Military Academy at West Point.The visit was part of his military education. Gettysburg was not simply a historic landscape to the young officers studying there.The battlefield offered a practical setting in which they could examine decisions made during the 1863 battle, look at the terrain and consider how armies had operated across it.Three years later, Eisenhower returned under very different circumstances.The First World War was underway, and Capt. Eisenhower had hoped to serve overseas. Instead, he was assigned to Camp Colt, a US Army Tank Corps training centre established on part of the Gettysburg battlefield. His responsibilities were straightforward but substantial: prepare volunteers, organise and train them, equip the men and have them ready for service abroad.He arrived with his wife, Mamie, and their first son. The posting meant that Gettysburg, briefly a place he had known as a cadet, became part of the Eisenhower family's early life.Camp Colt was eventually disbanded after the war, and Eisenhower moved on. His military career would take him far beyond Pennsylvania. Over the following decades, he served in a succession of assignments and eventually became one of the senior American commanders of the Second World War.After the Second World War, Eisenhower's life had changed considerably. He had become an internationally recognised military commander and, after leaving active military service, served as president of Columbia University.He and Mamie began looking for a place where they could eventually retire. Gettysburg naturally held a particular attraction.In 1950, they purchased a 189-acre farm adjoining the Gettysburg battlefield. The property had belonged to Allen Redding, whose family later recalled how proud he was to have sold the farm to Eisenhower.The purchase did not immediately give the couple the quiet retirement they had imagined. Eisenhower soon accepted another demanding role, leaving the United States to take command of NATO in Europe.The farm remained, waiting for a later chapter. That chapter began in earnest after Eisenhower returned to the United States and entered the 1952 presidential race. The property became part of his Pennsylvania political campaign from the beginning. State Republican leaders were invited to a picnic there, turning what was intended as a home into a setting for an early gathering with political allies.Yet the farm was never simply a political property.When Eisenhower became president in 1953, the Gettysburg farm was still not ready to serve as the comfortable weekend retreat the couple wanted.The original house had serious structural problems. Much of it had to be removed, and the property underwent extensive renovation. Work was completed in March 1955.From then on, the Eisenhowers began spending weekends and holidays there whenever the demands of the presidency allowed.The setting was familiar territory for Eisenhower, but the scale of his responsibilities had changed dramatically since his days at Camp Colt. He was now responsible for the executive branch and dealing with international crises, yet the farm provided a degree of distance from Washington that was difficult to find elsewhere. His routine there reflected both sides of his life.There were ordinary farm activities and leisure. Eisenhower played golf at the Gettysburg Country Club, spent time at his skeet range and took an interest in the Angus cattle he kept on the property.The farm became particularly important in 1955, when Eisenhower suffered a heart attack. During his recovery, the property served for a period as the "Temporary White House". That meant that the quiet rural surroundings were accompanied by the machinery of government. Eisenhower continued to receive briefings and conduct business while recuperating.His mornings often began with information about events around the world. Staff meetings could take place at the farm, and important matters still reached him there. The arrangement was unusual in appearance but practical in some respects. Eisenhower could step away from Washington without completely stepping away from the presidency.The farm also became a place where he could meet people away from the formal atmosphere of the White House.Visitors included political figures and foreign leaders. Some meetings began at Camp David before guests travelled on to Gettysburg. Once there, Eisenhower could show them the farm, including the Angus cattle and barns, before settling with them on the porch of the house.Eisenhower later explained that the informal surroundings helped him understand the people he was dealing with and what he called "the other man's equation". The setting removed some of the ceremony that normally surrounded meetings with a president. A farm visit could become a diplomatic conversation.Eisenhower left the presidency in January 1961 after two terms in office. For the first time in decades, he and Mamie could live according to something closer to their own timetable.They returned to the Gettysburg farm permanently as their retirement home. Eisenhower was still far from an idle retiree.During the week, he worked from an office at Gettysburg College. He wrote and worked on his memoirs, while his position as a former president and former Allied commander meant that political figures and business leaders continued to seek his advice.He also remained connected to international affairs. World leaders still visited him, and successive presidents could draw on his experience. The distinction was that he was no longer required to make the final decisions from the Oval Office.At the farm, the rhythm of life was different.Family visits, friends, cattle and time outdoors became more important parts of the day. The property had begun as a place they bought with retirement in mind, but by the 1960s it had become something more permanent: the centre of their private life.For Eisenhower, the landscape also carried a long personal history.He had first seen Gettysburg as a cadet. He had returned as a young officer during the First World War. Decades later, he was living beside the same battlefield after serving as one of the most prominent American military commanders of his generation and as president of the United States.The Eisenhowers decided not to keep the property as a private family estate indefinitely.In 1967, General and Mrs Eisenhower donated their home and farm to the National Park Service. The decision ensured that the property would eventually become accessible as a historic site rather than remaining solely a private residence.Eisenhower died two years later, in 1969, at the age of 78. Mamie remained at Gettysburg.There had been suggestions that she move to Washington, where she would have been closer to relatives and friends. She chose instead to continue living at the farm. For another decade, the house remained her home.She died in 1979. The following year, the National Park Service opened the property to the public.The Eisenhower National Historic Site occupies an unusual place alongside the battlefield that first brought the future president to Gettysburg.The Civil War landscape around it is associated with armies, commanders and the events of July 1863. The Eisenhower property tells a much later story. Its history is tied to military service too, but also to presidential life, diplomatic meetings, retirement and family routines. The connection between the two is difficult to miss.Eisenhower first came to Gettysburg to study a battle fought generations earlier. His second visit placed him in the middle of another war, training soldiers for a conflict that was then still unfolding. After that came a career that carried him across the United States and Europe, culminating in the presidency. Yet after all those movements, he returned to Gettysburg.The farm gave him a place where cattle could occupy the same landscape as presidential briefings, where foreign dignitaries could sit on a porch after touring a barn, and where the former commander of Allied forces could spend time with family away from the formal institutions that had defined much of his public life.For nearly two decades, the property was both a retreat and a workplace. In retirement, it became home.
Article Summary: Dwight D. Eisenhower visited Gettysburg as a West Point cadet in 1915. Three years later, he was back, now a young Army officer assigned to Camp Colt, a tank training centre established on the battlefield. In 1950, he and Mamie bought a 189-acre farm beside the battlefield and it would become their retirement home and the place where Eisenhower spent his final years.

Article Title: ‘Fundamentally differed’: US military newspaper publisher quits amid Pentagon row over editorial freedom
Article Text:
The Pentagon has increasingly criticised the newspaper’s coverage. AP

The longtime publisher of Stars and Stripes, the US military newspaper, has resigned amid growing disagreements with the Pentagon over the publication’s editorial independence and direction.According to Al Jazeera, Max D Lederer Jr announced his retirement in a memo to staff on Tuesday, saying his understanding of the newspaper’s mission differed fundamentally from the direction being pursued by the US department of defense.Lederer said his leadership philosophy and understanding of the value of Stars and Stripes were no longer aligned with the Pentagon’s vision for the organisation. His resignation comes as the administration of President Donald Trump seeks greater control over the newspaper’s editorial direction.Founded in 1861, Stars and Stripes has long served US military personnel and their families, including troops stationed overseas. Although it receives significant government funding, the publication has historically maintained editorial independence from the administrations in power.The Pentagon has increasingly criticised the newspaper’s coverage. Defense secretary Pete Hegseth has accused Stars and Stripes of promoting what he described as “woke distractions”, while the Trump administration has objected to reports highlighting poor conditions and declining morale among US service members.The newspaper came under particular scrutiny after reporting on problems aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, a US aircraft carrier involved in the ongoing war with Iran. Stars and Stripes was among two military publications to report on falling morale and suicide attempts involving service members aboard the carrier.The Pentagon announced in January that it wanted to bring Stars and Stripes into closer alignment with government priorities. Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell described the move as an effort to return the publication to its “original mission” of reporting for US warfighters.The administration also removed Jacqueline Smith, the newspaper’s ombudsman, whose role included protecting its editorial independence. Smith criticised the decision, warning that removing the official responsible for safeguarding editorial independence raised concerns about political interference.The dispute comes amid wider tensions between the Pentagon and the US media under Hegseth. The Defense department has introduced restrictions on journalists’ access to the Pentagon, while some of its media policies have faced legal challenges.Lederer’s resignation now adds to concerns over the future of Stars and Stripes and the extent to which a government-funded military newspaper can maintain editorial independence while operating under the Pentagon’s oversight.
Article Summary: Max D Lederer Jr announced his retirement in a memo to staff on Tuesday. Lederer said his leadership philosophy and understanding of the value of Stars and Stripes were no longer aligned with the Pentagon’s vision for the organisation. His resignation comes as the administration of President Donald Trump seeks greater control over the newspaper's editorial direction.

Article Title: Mistaken for intruders: Reporters, military personnel held at gunpoint at US Space Force base
Article Text:
The Vandenberg space force base near Santa Barbara, California

Five reporters and two military personnel invited to an event at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California were briefly detained at gunpoint after security officers mistook them for people attempting to enter the base without authorisation.According to The Guardian, the incident took place on Monday ahead of an invitation-only groundbreaking ceremony for a new training facility for missile operators at the federal airfield near Santa Barbara. Reporters from Noozhawk and KEYT were among those detained, with both outlets later reporting details of the incident.The group was travelling in a government minivan as part of a convoy escorted by uniformed public affairs personnel when security officers suddenly ordered them out of their vehicles with their hands raised. Guns were drawn, sirens sounded and barricades were placed at the entrance, KEYT reported.The two military personnel assigned to the base, an enlisted member and a junior officer, were handcuffed and placed in military vehicles. The civilian reporters were ordered to sit on a curb, according to Noozhawk.Reporters from KSBY-TV and the Santa Maria Times/Lompoc Record were also among those detained. The group was held for more than 30 minutes and missed the scheduled event before being released without further incident.A Space Launch Delta 30 public affairs spokesperson described the episode as a breakdown in communication, while stressing that the base had recently experienced an increase in attempted unauthorised entries.“Every potential unauthorized presence must be treated as a legitimate threat until proven otherwise,” the spokesperson told Noozhawk, adding that the security of the base and its personnel remained the priority.Tom Bolton, editor in chief of Noozhawk, said the outlet respected the military's security requirements but described the incident as unfortunate and unnecessary, particularly because firearms were drawn.Bolton said he hoped to meet base leadership to review the incident and discuss measures to prevent a similar situation from occurring again.
Article Summary: Five reporters and two military personnel were briefly detained at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. Security officers mistook them for people attempting to enter the base without authorisation. The incident took place on Monday ahead of an invitation-only groundbreaking ceremony for a new training facility for missile operators.

Article Title: Meet Delaney Peterson, the Florida student who spent three years turning recycled glass into artificial reefs designed to give oysters a new home
Article Text:
​Representative Image of oyster larvae attaching to porous structures made from recycled glass in a coastal habitat (AI-generated image)

Why recycled foamed glass could be useful for rebuilding oyster habitat

What Delaney Peterson achieved at Regeneron ISEF 2026

Why recycled materials are attracting attention in oyster restoration

Delaney Peterson, a student at Belleview High School in Ocala, Florida, spent three years developing a science project around a deceptively simple question: could discarded glass be transformed into a material suitable for rebuilding oyster habitat? Her project, titled Revolutionising Artificial Reefs: Recycled Foamed Glass Aggregates as a Sustainable Solution for Oyster Habitats, reached its third year in 2026 and earned third place in the Earth and Environmental Sciences category at the Regeneron International Science and Engineering Fair (ISEF), one of the world's largest science competitions for high school students. Peterson also received a special award from the Florida Institute of Technology that included a four-year full-tuition scholarship if she chooses to attend the university full-time. Her research focuses on recycled foamed glass aggregate, a lightweight, porous material made from processed glass, and investigates its potential for use in artificial reef structures. Rather than treating the work as a one-off science fair experiment, Peterson returned to the same research question over three consecutive years, developing the project through successive stages before taking it to the international level.Foamed glass aggregate is produced by processing recycled glass into a lightweight material with a porous internal structure. The material has applications in construction and other engineering projects because of properties such as its low weight and durability, while its porous structure gives it characteristics that differ from conventional solid materials. Those features could potentially be useful in oyster restoration because oyster larvae need hard surfaces on which to attach and grow.Artificial oyster reefs are commonly constructed using materials such as oyster shell, limestone and concrete, but researchers have also investigated engineered alternatives that could provide suitable surfaces while making use of waste materials. Peterson's project explores recycled foamed glass within that broader context, bringing together two environmental challenges: the need to divert discarded glass into useful applications and the need to create additional hard substrate for oyster habitat. The publicly available information on Peterson's specific project, however, does not provide enough technical detail to establish that her particular material has already been proven to outperform conventional reef substrates or successfully establish a functioning oyster reef, so those claims should not be made without further project documentation.Peterson's project received recognition at multiple levels before reaching the international competition. According to Society for Science's official 2026 special awards announcement, she received the Florida Institute of Technology's special award and its four-year full-tuition scholarship. She also earned third place in the Earth and Environmental Sciences category in the ISEF Grand Awards, a substantially broader recognition of the project than the university-specific scholarship alone. Her research had previously advanced through the Big Springs Regional Science Fair, qualifying her to compete at ISEF alongside some of the strongest young researchers from around the world. The three-year development of the project is particularly notable because Peterson was not simply presenting a single experiment created for the 2026 competition; she had continued working on the same research problem across multiple years. That progression allowed her to take an initial idea about recycled materials and develop it into a project that ultimately received both an international category placement and a major university scholarship.Oyster reefs are important coastal ecosystems because oysters filter water, provide habitat for other marine organisms and can help stabilise shorelines. Their decline in many coastal areas has encouraged restoration programmes to investigate materials that can provide the hard surfaces oysters need to establish new colonies. Peterson's project approaches that challenge from a circular-economy perspective: instead of treating discarded glass solely as waste, it investigates whether the material can be processed into something potentially useful for habitat restoration. Her award demonstrates that the project was judged highly at ISEF, but it does not by itself establish that the material is ready for deployment in real oyster reefs. The publicly accessible Society for Science information confirms the project's title, three-year development and awards, but does not provide the detailed methodology and experimental results needed to evaluate its real-world performance. Those limitations make it important to separate what has been demonstrated from what remains a research possibility. What is clear is that Peterson has spent three years pursuing an unconventional environmental engineering question and took it far enough to earn third place among ISEF's Earth and Environmental Sciences projects, while also receiving a four-year tuition scholarship an unusually strong result for a high-school research project that began with the idea of giving discarded glass a second life underwater.
Article Summary: Delaney Peterson, a student at Belleview High School in Ocala, Florida, spent three years developing a science project around a deceptively simple question. Her project, titled Revolutionising Artificial Reefs: Recycled Foamed Glass Aggregates as a Sustainable Solution for Oyster Habitats, reached its third year in 2026. It earned third place in the Earth and Environmental Sciences category at the Regeneron International Science and Engineering Fair. Peterson also received a special award from the Florida Institute of Technology that included a four-year full-tuition scholarship.

Article Title: Trump announces ‘most crushing’ economic operation against Iran, warns countries aiding Tehran
Article Text:
Donald Trump warns Iran

Trump warns countries aiding Iran

US expands economic pressure campaign

War and Hormuz dispute deepen tensions

US President Donald Trump on Wednesday announced what he called the “most crushing economic operation” ever imposed against a country, targeting Iran with an unprecedented campaign of economic warfare and isolation while warning nations providing Tehran with financial or commercial support of “tremendous” consequences.Trump said the new measures would target any country whose financial institutions, businesses, airports or government entities provide what he described as a “lifeline” to Iran. He did not specify what penalties Washington would impose or name any country that could be targeted.“No one has given the Islamic Republic of Iran a greater opportunity to make a Deal than me. TRAGICALLY, for them, they have failed to take it. Therefore, today, I am announcing the MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY! This will be Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.“Today, I am also announcing that ANY country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences.Oil smuggling, swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries, front companies — It all needs to stop NOW.
