You know who you are,” he said.The announcement marks a further escalation of Washington's economic campaign against Tehran as the US war with Iran approaches its sixth month, with the dispute over the Strait of Hormuz continuing to complicate efforts to reach a broader settlement.Trump called for an immediate halt to activities including “oil smuggling, swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries” and the use of “front companies” to support Iran.“This will be an ECONOMIC D-DAY, and we need all of our Allies to stand with the United States of America to isolate, and defeat, the Iran threat. These maniacs are on the ropes, and these HISTORIC MEASURES will cripple them and their ability to project terror worldwide,” Trump said.He also claimed that Iran's military capabilities had been severely weakened by the conflict.“Their navy is gone, their air force is destroyed, their military factories are now rubble, their currency is worthless, and their country is hanging by a thread,” Trump said.Trump also repeated his warning over Iran's nuclear programme, saying: “IRAN WILL NEVER HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON.”Before the war began, China, India, Turkey, Germany, South Korea and Japan were among Iran's major trading partners. Trump did not identify any of these countries as a target of the new measures.Trump's announcement follows comments by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that Washington would intensify efforts to isolate Iran economically.“It will be a combination of economic isolation, like the world has never seen before,” Bessent told Newsmax last week.The US Treasury has also been pursuing a sanctions campaign known as Operation Economic Fury, aimed at cutting off Tehran's sources of revenue through targeted measures.Trump's latest announcement appears to widen that pressure by warning not only Iranian entities but also foreign governments and businesses that continue providing financial, commercial or logistical support to Tehran.The president did not provide details on how the new campaign would be implemented or whether it would involve secondary sanctions against foreign companies and financial institutions.The conflict began on February 28, when US and Israeli forces launched strikes against Iran. Tehran responded with missile and drone attacks against US and Israeli targets across the Middle East.The Strait of Hormuz has remained at the centre of the confrontation. The strategic waterway is a major route for global energy shipments and has faced severe disruption during the conflict.Trump has maintained that the strait remains open despite the wider confrontation.“There are no talks or conversations going on, or scheduled, with the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump said in a Truth Social post on Tuesday.“The Naval Blockade remains in full force and effect. The Hormuz Strait is open and operating. All water mines have been removed or detonated,” he added.His remarks came a day after his son-in-law and special envoy Jared Kushner said talks with Iran were still under way and were “probably more robust” than they had ever been.Iranian Parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has said Tehran would not reopen the Strait until Washington meets its demands, including lifting the blockade, releasing frozen Iranian assets and easing oil sanctions.The widening gap between Trump's claims that negotiations are not taking place and reports of continuing contacts has added uncertainty over whether the conflict can be brought to an end.Trump has previously said negotiations could resume “maybe at some point”, while insisting that Iran must not be allowed to develop a nuclear weapon.“Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon. You know why? Because they'd use it. And we're not going to let them use it. So Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon, and they won't,” he said.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump warns countries aiding Iran of 'tremendous consequences' New measures will target any country whose financial institutions, businesses, airports or government entities provide what he described as a 'lifeline' to Iran. He did not specify what penalties Washington would impose or name any country that could be targeted. Announcement marks a further escalation of Washington's economic campaign against Tehran.

Article Title: Meet Alex Webster, the Florida teenager who is giving away mangroves as ‘pets’ to people to protect disappearing coastal forests
Article Text:
Image Credit: Courtesy of Alex Webster

How is Alex Webster making mangroves feel like pets

Why are mangroves so important

Mangroves. Image Credit: Wikipedia

Can a simple idea change how people see conservation

Mangroves may not be the first thing that comes to mind when people think about a pet, but Florida teenager Alex Webster is turning that idea into a unique environmental mission. Through the ‘ My Pet Mangrove programme ’, Alex is encouraging people to form a personal connection with these important coastal forests and help keep them protected. The National Geographic Society describes mangroves as coastal forests that store carbon, protect coastlines and help fight climate change. It also highlights Webster’s programme as an effort to ensure these ecosystems remain protected. The idea stands out because it gives conservation a more personal face. Instead of seeing mangroves as distant forests, people can think of them as something they can care about and help preserve. Webster’s work has earned recognition as one of the National Geographic Society’s 2026 Slingshot Challenge Award recipients.The answer is in the name itself, ‘My Pet Mangrove.’ The National Geographic Society presents Webster’s project as a creative way of protecting mangrove ecosystems. The programme uses the idea of having a mangrove as a pet, transforming an environmental issue into something more familiar and personal.Rather than relying only on facts about climate change or coastal protection, the concept gives people a different reason to care. A pet is something that is looked after, valued and remembered. Applying that idea to a mangrove can make conservation feel less distant and more immediate. The project therefore connects an everyday idea with a much larger environmental challenge. It suggests that protecting nature does not always have to begin with a large organisation or a complicated campaign. Sometimes, it can start by helping someone develop a simple emotional connection with the natural world.Mangroves occupy a special place along coastlines, where land meets the sea. They are more than simply collections of trees growing near water. According to the National Geographic Society, these coastal forests store carbon, protect coastlines and help fight climate change. That makes their survival important not only for the plants and animals that depend on them, but also for people living near the coast. Mangroves form a natural part of coastal environments, and their ability to help protect shorelines gives them a role that reaches far beyond their appearance. But protecting an ecosystem can sometimes feel like an abstract task. People may understand that forests matter without feeling personally connected to a particular one. Webster’s approach takes a different route by making mangroves something people can relate to on an individual level.Mangroves can be discussed through large subjects such as carbon storage, climate change and coastal protection. Those subjects are important, but they can also feel distant from everyday life. By giving mangroves a more familiar identity as pets, Webster’s programme offers another way of starting that conversation. The National Geographic Society specifically says Webster’s programme is making sure these ecosystems remain protected. That description highlights the central purpose of the project of encouraging people to value mangroves so that they are more likely to care about their future.There is no complicated message at the heart of the project. It is about making an important ecosystem easier to understand and care about. Webster’s My Pet Mangrove is memorable precisely because it is unusual. A mangrove is not an obvious pet, and that unexpected comparison can make people stop and think. By giving people a more personal way to think about these ecosystems, the Florida teenager is showing that environmental action can begin with something as simple as caring about a tree.
Article Summary: Florida teenager Alex Webster is turning the idea of a mangrove into a unique environmental mission. The National Geographic Society describes mangroves as coastal forests that store carbon, protect coastlines and help fight climate change. The idea stands out because it gives conservation a more personal face.

Article Title: After Great Northern Paper Company shut down in 2008, Maine’s Millinocket lost more than jobs; locals now look to tourism, small businesses and new industry for revival
Article Text:
Once a thriving paper mill town, Millinocket is now looking to tourism and small businesses for its future.

A town built around the paper mill

‘It took the life out of everybody in town’

Locals remember the jobs, community and stability that Great Northern Paper Company brought to Millinocket.

‘This was my life’

From ‘Magic City’ to a tourism economy

From a paper industry powerhouse to a tourism destination, Millinocket is navigating an uncertain new chapter.

A shrinking school, but a strong community

Small businesses are keeping the town alive

‘We’re an analog stronghold in the digital world’

‘It’s the loss of a dream’

A community waiting for its next chapter

Millinocket, Maine, was once a quintessential company town built around the paper industry. For generations, the Great Northern Paper Company provided jobs, stability and a sense of community to thousands of residents. But when the mill shut down in 2008, the impact went far beyond job losses, changing the town’s economy, population and identity.YouTuber Peter Santenello explored the town and its history in a recent episode on his Peter Santenello YouTube channel, meeting longtime residents and business owners to understand what happened to the community after the mill’s closure.Santenello met Dick, a longtime Millinocket resident who was closely associated with the paper mill and was involved when it eventually shut down. As he took Santenello through the former mill property, Dick recalled how deeply the company was woven into everyday life.According to Dick, Great Northern Paper Company owned virtually all the real estate in the town at one point. The company helped employees build homes by providing labour for foundations and other construction work.“When the company left, it was deeded over,” Dick explained during Santenello’s tour.The relationship between the company and the community extended beyond housing. The paper company was also a major taxpayer and supported local institutions, including schools.Dick recalled that his wife, who trained as a teacher, eventually secured a teaching position in Millinocket that was among the highest-paid teaching jobs in Maine at the time.“The paper company was the majority taxpayer, and they didn't hesitate if the school needed something,” he told Santenello.The most painful memories, however, remain tied to the mill’s closure.Dick recalled being told that the mill would remain open if workers could demonstrate profitability for two months. According to his account, employees worked hard to meet that target and succeeded.“We busted our tails to keep it operating and make a profit,” Dick said.He recalled that the mill showed a profit in both months, with the second month being particularly strong. Yet, in September, workers were told the operation would close.“Corporate said that they didn't feel that we could sustain that profitability,” Dick recalled.The closure, he said, “took the life out of everybody in town.”The former mill worker also suggested that competition with Fraser Paper in Madawaska may have played a role, although he acknowledged that this was the explanation workers could make sense of at the time.Walking through the abandoned mill appeared to be particularly emotional for Dick.“This was my life,” he told Santenello while looking at the machinery he had worked around for decades.He recalled spending long hours monitoring the machinery and supervising shutdowns, sometimes walking miles around the enormous paper machine to check on crews.“I loved my job. I loved the people I worked with,” he said.For Dick, the people were ultimately what made the work meaningful.“The job is a job. The people make the job,” he said.He also became emotional while looking at the walls inside the mill, reflecting on generations of his family who had worked there.“You look at this wall and you say, my father could have touched this wall. My grandfather could have touched this wall,” he said.Millinocket was once known as the “Magic City” because, as Dick explained, it essentially grew out of the woods around the paper industry.“Everybody had something to do in Millinocket,” he said.Today, however, the town is increasingly turning toward tourism and outdoor recreation. Its proximity to Mount Katahdin and the Appalachian Trail has helped attract hikers, seasonal residents and outdoor enthusiasts.But Dick believes tourism alone cannot replace the kind of wages and economic stability provided by manufacturing.“You need them both. People have to recreate. But people have to earn a living too,” he told Santenello.“And you have to have a balance.”The scale of Millinocket’s decline is visible in its schools. Dick recalled that his graduating class had around 356 students. By comparison, he estimated that the graduating class in 2026 had just 35 students.Yet the town still retains a strong sense of community.Millinocket’s football team won a state championship, providing an unexpected boost to local morale.“The houses in town are just houses. They're just a structure. It's the people,” Dick said. “The people are what really makes the difference.”Santenello also spoke with local business owners, including Jamie, who runs a company producing products from reclaimed wood.Jamie explained that the business employs around 20 people and sells products outside Millinocket, including through Amazon, because the local population alone cannot support a large customer base.He also acknowledged the enormous economic hole left by the mill.“The mill brought in hundreds of jobs. We don't have anything that's replaced that,” Jamie said.Another local resident, electrician Joe, told Santenello that he had worked at the mill before its closure. After being laid off at the age of 48, he went back to college and trained as an electrician, with his education paid for through assistance available to displaced workers.His story reflects one of the ways former mill workers adapted after the industry's collapse.Santenello also visited the Blue Ox Saloon, a longtime downtown business whose history is intertwined with Millinocket.Owner Andrew explained that his father bought the building in 1988 when it was condemned and spent years rebuilding it before opening the bar in 1994.The business once benefited from the thousands of workers employed by the mill. Andrew recalled that when his father opened the establishment, there were seven bars along the same street and the Blue Ox could have customers lined up outside.Today, business is considerably different, but his family has no intention of giving up.“I'll never give up,” Andrew told Santenello.He described the town as being in a difficult transition, while expressing hope that a new generation could help revive it.Santenello's conversation with Andrew offered perhaps the clearest description of Millinocket's psychological struggle.The town, he observed, was created around the mill and grew because of it. When the mill disappeared, the community was left grieving not simply an industry but an entire way of life.“It's the loss of a dream. A loss of a life unlived,” Andrew said.At the same time, he believes the town's resilience could eventually lead to a revival.“There's young energy coming in,” he said, pointing to efforts to renovate parts of downtown.While walking through Millinocket, Santenello observed the contrast between vacant buildings, renovated properties, small businesses and homes that residents continue to maintain.There are also hopes for new industry. Residents mentioned the possibility of developments including a salmon farm, while the nonprofit Our Katahdin is working toward finding new uses for the former mill site.But for many residents, the future remains uncertain.As Dick put it, tourism can bring visitors and economic activity, but it cannot necessarily replace the high-paying manufacturing jobs that once supported generations of families.“If you don't have that balance, you're gonna have just a community pass-through where people come to recreate and leave,” he said.Santenello ended his visit reflecting on Millinocket's unusual combination of decline, nostalgia and resilience.“Interesting past, unknown future, great people we met today,” he said at the conclusion of his video.For a town once built around paper, Millinocket is now searching for what comes next.
Article Summary: Millinocket, Maine, was once a quintessential company town built around the paper industry. For generations, the Great Northern Paper Company provided jobs, stability and a sense of community to thousands of residents. When the mill shut down in 2008, the impact went far beyond job losses, changing the town’s economy, population and identity.

Article Title: MacKenzie Scott got $1,000 from her roommate to stay in college. Five years later, she donated $26 billion to charity
Article Text:
MacKenzie Scott remembers the roommate who helped her stay in college with $1,000

From Toni Morrison’s student to a novelist: Scott’s career took a major turn after 2019

How a $1,000 loan grew into a mission to help students

The $1,000 loan became part of Scott’s larger giving philosophy

From a $1,000 loan to a legacy of giving

MacKenzie Scott is now known for giving billions of dollars to charities, but her own experience of needing financial help began much earlier. While studying at Princeton, Scott faced a difficult period when money was tight and remaining at university was uncertain. Her roommate, Jeannie Ringo Tarkenton, noticed her struggle and lent her $1,000, helping Scott continue her education.At the time, it was simply a friend helping another student through a difficult moment. Scott later remembered the gesture as one of the acts of kindness that shaped her outlook on giving. The story took an unexpected turn years later when Tarkenton went on to create Funding U, a company offering education loans to students who may struggle to qualify for traditional private loans. What began as a modest loan between roommates eventually became part of a much larger story about education, financial support and philanthropy.Scott arrived at Princeton with ambitions that would eventually take her into both literature and business. Money, however, could become a serious problem. During her sophomore year, she was struggling financially and faced the possibility of leaving university.According to Fortune, her roommate, Jeannie Ringo Tarkenton, noticed what was happening.Rather than treating it as someone else’s problem, she lent Scott $1,000. It was a relatively small amount compared with the fortunes Scott would later give away, but its significance was tied to the timing. The money helped Scott continue her studies at a point when an interruption could have changed the direction of her life.Scott has since described the incident as one of several acts of kindness she remembers when considering the people who influenced her. In an essay published through Yield Giving, she also recalled receiving free dental treatment from a local dentist after breaking a tooth while she was at college.Those experiences became part of her understanding of how assistance can work. Help does not always arrive as a large grant or a formal programme. Sometimes it comes from a person who happens to be nearby when someone needs it.Scott graduated from Princeton and went into writing, studying under the novelist Toni Morrison. Her literary career preceded the period when she became widely known for philanthropy.In 2005, she published The Testing of Luther Albright, her first novel. The book later received the American Book Award, and Morrison praised it for its emotional and literary qualities.Her career took a very different turn in the public eye after her marriage to Jeff Bezos ended in 2019. As part of the divorce settlement, Scott received a substantial holding in Amazon, giving her the financial resources to become a major philanthropist.The scale of her giving grew rapidly. Since 2020, she has directed billions of dollars towards organisations working across areas such as education, racial and gender equity, disaster recovery and community development.Tarkenton did not simply remain a footnote in Scott’s story. About two decades after lending her roommate the money, she went on to establish Funding U, a company designed to provide education loans to students who might struggle to qualify for conventional private lending because they do not have a cosigner.The connection between the two women is striking largely because the original loan was so ordinary. Tarkenton had helped someone she knew personally. Later, she applied a similar principle on a much larger scale to students facing financial barriers.Funding U has since provided about $80 million in low-interest loans to roughly 8,000 students, according to Princeton.Tarkenton has been reluctant to portray herself as the person responsible for Scott’s later success. In an interview with the Princeton Alumni Weekly, she suggested that Scott would probably have found a way to finish university anyway.Her point was less about claiming credit than about recognising how small acts of assistance can accumulate. For Scott, the $1,000 mattered because it arrived at a moment when she needed it.Scott’s philanthropic approach has grown into something far removed from that college loan. Through Yield Giving, the platform she established in 2022, she has directed billions of dollars to thousands of organisations.Her method has also attracted attention because many of the recipients are relatively small or community-based groups rather than only the largest charitable institutions. The money is often intended to give organisations room to decide how best to use it.By early 2026, Scott had given roughly $26 billion through her philanthropy, according to Fortune, while continuing to hold a large personal fortune.Yet when Scott reflected on what had shaped her attitude towards giving, she did not point only to the enormous sums involved. She remembered individual people.The college roommate who found her crying and lent her $1,000 was among them.Tarkenton once helped one student remain at university. Years later, she created a business aimed at helping thousands of other students finance their education. Scott, meanwhile, went on to distribute billions of dollars to organisations across the United States and beyond.Neither path began with a grand philanthropic plan. The first step was simply responding to a person who needed help.That is perhaps why the old story has remained relevant to Scott. The amount itself was modest. What mattered was that someone acted when the need was immediate, without knowing what that decision might eventually lead to.For Tarkenton, the experience also offered a personal example of what financial support can mean to a student without an easy safety net. For Scott, it became one of the memories she carried into a very different financial life.The $1,000 was eventually dwarfed by the billions Scott was able to give away. But it was never really about the size of the check. It was about what happened when someone decided that another person’s education was worth helping to protect.
Article Summary: MacKenzie Scott’s career took a major turn after her marriage to Jeff Bezos ended in 2019. As part of the divorce settlement, Scott received a substantial holding in Amazon, giving her the financial resources to become a major philanthropist. Since 2020, she has directed billions of dollars towards organisations working across areas such as education, racial and gender equity, disaster recovery and community development.

Article Title: In the 1980s, Burmese pythons invaded Florida’s Everglades, and decades later raccoons fell 99.3%, opossums 98.9% and bobcats 87.5%
Article Text:
How Burmese pythons invaded themselves in Florida

How pythons hunt in the Everglades

The animals once common in the Everglades grew scarce

The wildlife decline matched the snakes' expansion

A hidden hunter with a wide range of prey

The real victims are the Everglades' native animals

A difficult problem in a very large landscape

For years, the Everglades was known for its tangled wetlands, alligators and an abundance of smaller mammals moving through the vegetation. Then an animal from south-east Asia began spreading through the marshes. Burmese pythons, most likely introduced through the pet trade, have established a breeding population in southern Florida and now occupy large parts of the Everglades. Their presence has coincided with an extraordinary change in some native mammal populations. Raccoons, opossums and bobcats have become far less common in areas where the snakes have been established for the longest time, while rabbits have virtually disappeared from some surveys.As reported by the American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS), a study based on more than 35,000 miles of surveys recorded declines of 99.3% in raccoons, 98.9% in opossums and 87.5% in bobcats since the late 1990s. The figures offer a glimpse of how one introduced predator has altered an entire wildlife community.Burmese pythons come from south-east Asia, thousands of miles from the sawgrass marshes and mangrove edges of southern Florida.Their arrival in the Everglades appears to have been tied to the exotic pet trade. Some snakes were probably released when owners could no longer manage them. Others may have escaped from captivity, including during storms and other disturbances. By the mid-1980s, there were signs that the species had begun establishing itself in the wild.That first foothold mattered because the Everglades offered conditions in which a large constrictor could survive and reproduce. Warm temperatures, extensive wetlands and abundant prey created a very different setting from a glass enclosure in someone's home.The result is now a self-sustaining population. There is no reliable figure for how many Burmese pythons occupy the Everglades. Estimates have ranged into the hundreds of thousands, although their secretive behaviour makes any population count difficult. The snakes spend much of their time hidden among vegetation or in water, and an animal that can grow to around 12 feet is surprisingly easy to miss in such a vast landscape.Burmese pythons are opportunistic hunters. They do not specialise in one particular type of animal, which is part of what makes their presence unusual in an ecosystem with a large variety of native wildlife.A python catches prey with its mouth and then wraps its muscular body around the animal. Once the prey has stopped breathing, the snake swallows it whole. There is no need to chase down another meal immediately; a large python can go for considerable periods between feeding.In Florida, its potential menu includes mammals, birds and reptiles. That range brings the snake into contact with species that evolved without having to contend with a giant constrictor as a regular predator. The concern is not limited to common animals. Pythons have also been recorded eating species of conservation interest, including the endangered Key Largo woodrat.For some animals, the problem is compounded by the fact that they have relatively few places to escape. The Everglades is vast, but suitable habitat is not necessarily safe habitat. A python can move through marshes, canals and vegetation, waiting for an opportunity rather than pursuing prey across open ground.The clearest indication of the scale of the change came from surveys carried out in Everglades National Park between 2003 and 2011, as reported by AAAS. Scientists covered more than 35,000 miles of roads and tracks, recording mammals encountered along the way. It was not a simple headcount of animals in the entire park. Instead, the repeated surveys provided a way of comparing how frequently different species appeared over time and across areas with different histories of python invasion.USGS reported, Opossum sightings had fallen by 98.9% from earlier levels. Bobcat numbers were down 87.5%, while raccoons, once among the mammals most commonly encountered in the park, had declined by 99.3%.Rabbits were more difficult to interpret because the survey recorded none in the affected areas. A later examination of marsh rabbit mortality provided another piece of the picture, linking deaths of the animals with python predation and helping explain why rabbit populations had become so difficult to find.These were not small variations from one survey year to the next. The declines represented a substantial change in the mammal community.The most severe declines occurred towards the southern end of the park, the same broad area where Burmese pythons had been present for the longest period. In places where the snakes had arrived more recently, mammal populations had not fallen to the same extent.That difference gave scientists an unusually useful comparison. If the disappearance of mammals had been caused entirely by a factor affecting the whole Everglades, such as a major change in habitat or weather, there would be less reason to expect the losses to line up so closely with the history of python establishment. Instead, the pattern followed the expanding range of the invasive snake.Areas outside the park where pythons had not been recorded also retained healthier mammal populations.The evidence could not establish that every missing animal had been killed by a python. Wildlife populations respond to many pressures, and the researchers were careful about drawing a direct cause-and-effect conclusion from the survey data alone.But the geographic pattern, the timing and the known feeding habits of the snakes pointed in the same direction.It would be tempting to view Burmese pythons as filling the role of another large predator. The situation is more complicated than that. Native predators evolved alongside the other species in the Everglades and are part of a long-established ecological network. Burmese pythons arrived from a different continent and encountered prey that had no evolutionary history with them.Their hunting strategy also differs from that of many native predators. A large constrictor does not need to outrun an animal over long distances. It can remain concealed and strike when prey comes within reach.The snake's ability to consume a wide range of animals means its effect is spread across several groups at once. That broad diet is particularly significant in a wetland where many mammals are already restricted to patches of suitable habitat.The size of a Burmese python can make encounters with people unsettling, but the documented danger in the United States has largely involved captive snakes rather than wild animals.As reported by AAAS, at least nine people in the country have been killed by Burmese pythons since 1999, but those cases involved pet snakes. There has been no documented case of a wild-born Burmese python killing a person in the United States.For the Everglades, the more immediate ecological concern is what happens to the animals living around the snakes.A python does not need to attack a person to have a substantial effect on its surroundings. A raccoon disappearing from an area, a rabbit no longer appearing on a survey route, or an opossum becoming exceptionally rare may seem insignificant when considered separately. Across a large wetland, repeated losses of that kind can add up to a profound change in the animal community.Removing Burmese pythons is not straightforward. The Everglades is a huge, wet and densely vegetated environment, and the snakes are exceptionally good at avoiding detection.They can remain hidden for long periods, move through water and vegetation, and occupy areas that are difficult for people to reach. Their reproductive ability also means that removing individual snakes does not necessarily prevent the population from persisting.This makes the problem different from dealing with an isolated escaped animal. The species has established itself.Florida has used organised searches, trapping efforts and public programmes to find and remove Burmese pythons. Individual captures can be significant, but the sheer scale of the invaded landscape means there is no simple way to sweep the snakes out of the Everglades.The challenge is made harder by the fact that the animals being protected are often much easier to miss than the snakes themselves.
Article Summary: Burmese pythons, most likely introduced through the pet trade, have established a breeding population in southern Florida. Their presence has coincided with an extraordinary change in some native mammal populations. Raccoons, opossums and bobcats have become far less common in areas where snakes have been established for the longest time.

Article Title: A Mexican couple bought a failed coconut farm 30 years ago; the 346-acre wasteland is now a wildlife haven for turtles, dolphins and flamingos
Article Text:
PC: Image AI generated

How coconut disease devastated the Yucatán Peninsula and transformed El Cuyo

Image AI generated

How El Cuyo became a wildlife haven for flamingos, turtles and dolphin

How the 346-acre El Cuyo property could become a luxury eco-resort

Why the owners are selling their £87 million estate in Mexico

Three decades ago, a 346-acre stretch of land on Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula was little more than the remains of a failed coconut farm. Disease had swept through millions of palms across the region, leaving behind a stripped and barren landscape. Mónica Hernández and her husband, architect and painter Aníbal González, saw something different in the neglected property they bought at El Cuyo. They had noticed the flamingos and spoonbills living nearby and decided to let the landscape recover rather than rebuild the plantation that had been lost. Over the years, native vegetation returned and the coastal estate became a haven for wildlife, with sea turtles, dolphins and flamingos now part of its surroundings. The couple also developed plans for an eco-conscious luxury residential complex; after 30 years, they are putting the £87 million estate on the market while keeping a small piece for themselves.The condition of the property was tied to a wider problem affecting the Yucatán Peninsula. Millions of coconut palms had been damaged by an aggressive plant disease in the 1990s, leaving areas that had once been productive looking almost empty.El Cuyo was among the places where the effects were visible, but Hernández and González did not see the damaged landscape simply as a failed agricultural site. They were drawn to the wildlife around it, particularly the flamingos and spoonbills they encountered in the area.The couple put what Hernández described as “big money” into the secluded property around 30 years ago. Rather than trying to recreate the old coconut plantation, they allowed the landscape to change. Once the dead coconut trees were burnt, the original vegetation began returning, according to Hernández. That regeneration became part of what the couple were trying to preserve. The result was a private coastal estate where the surrounding natural environment became as important as the buildings and other improvements made to the land.The property now stretches across more than 346 acres, with roughly four miles of beachfront. Its setting on the northern Yucatán Peninsula puts it alongside a coastline already known for its wildlife, and the estate has become a place where animals are a regular part of the landscape rather than an attraction brought in for visitors. Flamingos and spoonbills were among the species that first caught the couple’s attention, while turtles and dolphins later became familiar sights around the property.Hernández told The Sun that dolphins arrive during certain seasons, describing their appearance as something unusual and beautiful. The couple also said they regularly spend time at the estate and enjoy seeing turtles and dolphins along the coast. The surrounding waters have helped shape the experience of El Cuyo, with wealthy visitors sometimes arriving by yacht and swimming towards the white beaches.The estate has since moved beyond being a private coastal retreat. Hernández and González received approval from the Mexican government for a residential development at El Cuyo, with the condition that the project follows ecological conservation requirements. Working with Casa e Progetti, they produced plans for a resort using renewable energy and natural resources rather than treating the surrounding environment as an afterthought.The proposed scheme includes 64 villas, each planned on plots ranging from 2.5 to 6.9 acres, with a section of private beachfront. The homes would average about 5,000 square feet and contain four or five bedrooms. Their design is intended to draw on Mayan architectural influences, with oval forms, open-air spaces, wooden structures and stone walls. The plans therefore combine a high-end residential development with an attempt to retain the character of the coastal setting.After three decades of developing the property, Hernández and González have decided that El Cuyo should pass to someone younger who can devote more time to the next stage of the project. According to The Sun, the estate is marketed by Beauchamp Estates and has an asking price of £87 million, which makes it the most expensive property in Mexican history. The couple do not intend to leave the place entirely, though. They plan to retain a smaller section at the edge of the estate for themselves.The decision is partly about time. Hernández is 75, and González is 81, and she said the project had previously demanded their attention “24/7”. They now want to spend more time at their own beach without having to manage the entire development. For Hernández, the future of the property is also tied to how its next owner treats the land. She said it would suit an ecologist and that whoever lives there should act as a guardian of nature.
Article Summary: Mónica Hernández and Aníbal González bought El Cuyo 30 years ago. They decided to let the landscape recover rather than rebuild the plantation that had been lost. Over the years, native vegetation returned and the coastal estate became a haven for wildlife. The couple also developed plans for an eco-conscious luxury residential complex. After 30 years, they are putting the £87 million estate on the market while keeping a small piece for themselves.

Article Title: Red-faced Pakistan summons top diplomat over US envoy Gor's J&K remark in Srinagar
Article Text:
US Ambassador Sergio Gor visits Srinagar with J&K CM Omar

Pakistan on Wednesday summoned the top US diplomat Islamabad and lodged a protest after US envoy to India Sergio Gor described Jammu and Kashmir as an “important part of India” during his visit to Srinagar on Wednesday.The remarks came as Gor made his first visit to Jammu and Kashmir since taking office and met chief minister Omar Abdullah.Gor’s comments were made during a joint media briefing with Abdullah following their meeting at the chief minister’s residence. “It’s a pleasure to be here. This is an important part of India. I am here, visiting for the first time. It is an incredibly beautiful place. I am thrilled to be here,” the US envoy said.Gor also indicated that Washington could reconsider its travel advisory for Jammu and Kashmir, saying the US regularly reviews its warnings. He said the Indian government and the Jammu and Kashmir administration had taken steps to improve safety in the region.“I cannot make any big announcements here today, but it is something we are going to look at,” Gor said, adding that the US would consider whether its existing travel warning should be downgraded.The ambassador also described his meeting with Abdullah as “very good” and said the two sides had discussed ways to deepen economic cooperation and create opportunities benefiting India and the US.Abdullah said the talks focused on what Washington could do for Jammu and Kashmir, while also referring to “certain legacy issues” that would need to be addressed.“We look forward to taking this conversation further,” Abdullah said, adding that he was “very hopeful and optimistic” that engagement between the US and Jammu and Kashmir would “both widen and deepen in the years ahead”.
Article Summary: Pakistan summons top US diplomat Islamabad and lodges a protest. US envoy to India Sergio Gor described Jammu and Kashmir as an “important part of India’ Gor also indicated that Washington could reconsider its travel advisory for J&K.

Article Title: Pakistan govt to challenge SC order to move jailed ex-PM Imran Khan to hospital
Article Text:
'Not within four walls of law': Pak law minister on Khan hospitalisation order

The Shehbaz Sharif-led Pakistan government will challenge the Supreme Court's order directing the transfer of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan to a private hospital, as law minister Azam Nazeer Tarar confirmed in a video message on Wednesday.According to news agency Reuters, the Pakitan Supreme Court had ordered the government to move Khan to Islamabad’s Shifa International Hospital within two days and allow him access to his personal physician.“This order is not within four walls of the law,” Tarar said in a video statement.He said authorities had reviewed the ruling and decided to approach the court seeking a review. “A convicted prisoner has to be treated either inside the jail or at a public hospital according to law,” Tarar said, adding that the review petition would seek a modification of the order.The move could end hopes of Imran Khan’s family and Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), which have repeatedly sought better healthcare and visitation rights for the former PM.It could also trigger public discontent over his treatment in custody.Recently, Imran Khan supporters staged widespread protest over Khan's imprisonment against Islamabad government.Khan, 73, has been jailed in Rawalpindi since August 2023 after being convicted in several cases that he says are politically motivated.He was removed from office in 2022 after falling out with Pakistan's powerful military establishment under army chief Asim Munir's influence.The Supreme Court order came after former president Arif Alvi raised concerns over World Cup winning captain and former PM's medical condition.Alvi also shared Khan's vitals on X.Imran Khan's sons have also repeatedly expressed concern about his deteriorating health, while his lawyers have claimed he suffered significant vision loss in his right eye while in prison.
Article Summary: Pakistani law minister Azam Nazeer Tarar confirms government will challenge the Supreme Court's order. Khan, 73, has been jailed in Rawalpindi since August 2023 after being convicted in several cases. He was removed from office in 2022 after falling out with Pakistan's powerful military establishment.

Article Title: 'Move Imran Khan to hospital': Pakistan Supreme Court directs govt amid ex-PM's health concerns
Article Text:
Pakistan SC orders Imran Khan’s hospital transfer. photo credit: AP

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe Imran Khan should receive immediate medical attention? Yes, he needs immediate care No, he can stay in jail Unsure, need more information 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Pakistan’s Supreme Court on Tuesday directed the government to move imprisoned former prime minister Imran Khan to a hospital, meeting a longstanding demand from his party and family amid growing concerns over his health.Khan, 73, has been in jail since August 2023 after being convicted in several cases that he and his supporters have described as politically motivated. His Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party welcomed the court order, saying it should have come earlier.“It’s a very welcome order and we wish it had happened sooner so his eye and general health would not have deteriorated this much,” PTI spokesperson Zulfikar Bukhari told Reuters.“He should remain in hospital until all doctors are satisfied,” Bukhari added.According to Khan’s spokesperson Naeem Haider Panjutha, the court directed that he be moved to Shifa International Hospital within 48 hours and remain there until September 16.Also Read: 'Needs to be moved to hospital now': Imran Khan's health in jail deteriorates The order came amid renewed concerns over Khan’s physical and mental health. His sons, Sulaiman Khan and Kasim Khan, have repeatedly raised concerns about his access to family, lawyers and doctors.“We have no updates because his family, doctors and lawyers haven’t been allowed to see him for seven months,” they told CNN earlier this month.The development came after former Pakistani president Arif Alvi also said on Tuesday that Khan’s medical reports were “alarming”, citing concerns over anxiety, palpitations and high blood pressure.In a post on X, Alvi said, “Imran Khan’s medical reports are alarming. I have gone through them with several specialists, and I am writing this in plain language so every Pakistani can understand exactly what is happening.”Alvi said the issues that concerned him most were Khan’s “anxiety and stress levels”, “palpitations,” and “high blood pressure”.Alvi also raised concerns over Khan’s heart rate and called for further medical monitoring, including a 24-hour Holter monitor.“I am deeply worried. Isolation is taking a physical toll on his body. If this is not addressed immediately, the damage may become irreversible with more complications to follow,” Alvi said.Calling for Khan to be hospitalised, the former president said: “@ImranKhanPTI definitely needs to be moved to a hospital environment now, under an independent panel of doctors.”Khan’s legal troubles intensified after his ouster as prime minister in a no-confidence vote in 2022. He has faced multiple cases, including those involving state gifts and an unlawful marriage, with some convictions suspended or overturned and appeals pending. He denies wrongdoing.The PTI, which came to power in 2018 and retains a significant support base, was stripped of its election symbol before the 2024 general election, forcing its candidates to contest as independents.
Article Summary: Pakistan's Supreme Court orders former prime minister Imran Khan to be moved to a hospital. Khan has been in jail since August 2023 after being convicted in several cases. His party welcomed the court order, saying it should have come earlier. The order came amid renewed concerns over Khan’s physical and mental health.

Article Title: 'Needs to be moved to hospital now': Imran Khan's health in jail deteriorates
Article Text:
Alvi warns over Imran Khan’s worsening health

NEW DELHI: Former Pakistan President Arif Alvi on Tuesday raised the alarm over jailed ex-PM Imran Khan’s worsening health, saying his medical reports were “alarming” and pointing to anxiety, heart palpitations and high blood pressure.In a post on X, Alvi said, "Imran Khan's medical reports are alarming. I have gone through them with several specialists, and I am writing this in plain language so every Pakistani can understand exactly what is happening."Alvi said the issues that concerned him most were Khan's "anxiety and stress levels", "palpitations," and "high blood pressure." He added that while sleeplessness was not mentioned in the report, Khan's medication appeared to suggest the problem."I have known Imran Khan for more than 35 years. Stress was never his weakness. That it is now at peak levels tells you everything about what three years of imprisonment and total isolation have done to him," he said.Alvi attributed Khan's stress to the political situation in Pakistan, the imprisonment and deaths of his colleagues, his own prolonged isolation and limited access to newspapers, books and information from outside.He also raised concerns over former PM and the only world-cup winning cricket captain Imran Khan's heart rate, which he said had increased to 54 beats per minute (bpm), compared with his historically lower resting rate."His heart rate is 54 bpm. Doctors will call that 'normal.' It is not normal for him," Alvi said, adding that Khan had also reported heart palpitations.Alvi called for Khan to undergo immediate cardiac monitoring, saying he "needs a 24-hour Holter monitor immediately". He also urged regular monitoring of his blood pressure.He recommended several tests, including a stress test, echocardiogram, cardiac MRI, cardiac artery calcium scan and cardiac CT angiogram, along with any other tests doctors may consider necessary."I am deeply worried. Isolation is taking a physical toll on his body. If this is not addressed immediately, the damage may become irreversible with more complications to follow," Alvi said.Calling for Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf founder Khan to be shifted to a hospital, Alvi said, "Imran Khan definitely needs to be moved to a hospital environment now, under an independent panel of doctors.""Neither his family nor the people of Pakistan trust government-appointed doctors alone," he added."The next three months will decide whether his condition is reversed or becomes permanent," Alvi said. He further said, "We all are alarmed. The country needs him more than ever before."Khan remains behind bars, while his sons, Sulaiman Khan and Kasim Khan, have also raised concerns about their father's access to his family, lawyers and doctors."We have no updates because his family, doctors and lawyers haven't been allowed to see him for seven months," they told CNN earlier this month.The statements came amid nationwide demonstrations by supporters of Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), who have demanded the release of the former prime minister and his wife, Bushra Bibi.Khan served as Pakistan's prime minister from 2018 until his ouster through a parliamentary no-confidence vote in 2022. He has been imprisoned since 2023 following convictions in several cases, including graft charges and the alleged disclosure of official secrets.Khan and his political aides have consistently alleged that the cases against him are politically motivated and intended to prevent his return to politics.After his ouster, Khan led nationwide rallies alleging that the government of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had conspired with Pakistan's military establishment and Washington to remove him. The subsequent crackdown targeted PTI leaders and supporters, while the party was barred from contesting the 2024 general elections.Khan's supporters have repeatedly maintained that the legal proceedings against him are politically motivated and aimed at blocking his political comeback.
Article Summary: Former Pakistan President Arif Alvi raises alarm over jailed ex-PM Imran Khan’s worsening health. Alvi says Khan's medical reports were “alarming” and pointed to anxiety, heart palpitations and high blood pressure. He also raised concerns over former PM's heart rate, which he said had increased to 54 beats per minute.

Article Title: '30 civilans killed': Baloch activist shares video of 'Pakistani war crime', seeks US intervention
Article Text:
Mir Yar Baloch has urged the US administration to impose sanctions on Pakistan.

Baloch leader seeks US sanctions

ALSO READ |

Pakistan disputes airstrike allegations

Protests erupt over reported civilian deaths

Mir Yar Baloch, a Baloch leader, has accused Pakistan 's military of carrying out an airstrike in Balochistan that allegedly killed 30 civilians, including women, children and infants.He claimed that video footage from the August 12 attack in Surab's Gidar Goandhan area provides evidence of the military operation and said he plans to take the matter to the International Criminal Court."The Republic of Balochistan has obtained video footage of the Surab Air Strike conducted by the external terrorist forces of Pakistan on 12th August, which killed 30 innocent Balochistan civilians including women, children, and infants and injured dozens more. The missile debris clearly visible in the video constitute irrefutable proof of Pakistan's terrorism. They also thoroughly expose Pakistan's military spokesperson, DG ISPR, who deliberately misled the global community on national media by claiming the attack was merely an IED blast on the ground," Mir Yar Baloch wrote on X.Mir Yar Baloch has urged the US administration to impose sanctions on Pakistan and halt military support, including F-16 engine spare parts and upgrades to fighter jets and missile programmes."The Republic of Balochistan urges the Trump administration to impose strict economic sanctions on Pakistan, cancel the delivery of spare parts for F-16 engines, and halt all upgradation package to its fighter jets and missile program.The Pakistan military and air force are massively employing these very weapons and aircraft against the people of the independent Republic of Balochistan. Washington must hold Pakistan fully accountable for its war crimes in Balochistan," he added.The two sides have given sharply different accounts of what happened in Surab, leaving the circumstances of the incident and the actual civilian death toll disputed.Pakistan's military has rejected the claim of an airstrike and said the casualties were caused by a premature explosion involving a vehicle-borne improvised explosive device allegedly being assembled by militants.The Inter-Services Public Relations said the initial blast killed eight militants and that a secondary explosion involving other explosives stored at the site also caused civilian deaths."However, the blast and secondary detonation of other explosives stored there by the terrorists of Indian Proxy have also reportedly caused tragic casualties of three nearby civilians," the ISPR said.The military said Pakistani forces and Balochistan Police subsequently killed 10 more individuals, taking the reported militant death toll to 18. Two Pakistani soldiers were also injured during the exchange of fire.The competing accounts have come amid protests in Balochistan following reports of civilian deaths in the Surab area.The Balochistan Post reported that more than 20 people were initially killed and at least 16 injured in the incident. Some local residents, however, claimed that the actual death toll could be higher.
Article Summary: Baloch leader Mir Yar Baloch has accused Pakistan's military of carrying out an airstrike in Balochistan that allegedly killed 30 civilians. He claims that video footage from the August 12 attack in Surab's Gidar Goandhan area provides evidence of the military operation. He has urged the US administration to impose sanctions on Pakistan.

Article Title: Pakistani minister in Balochistan province escapes armed attack on convoy
Article Text:
All six injured people suffered bullet wounds, according to a senior police official.​

Balochistan home minister Mir Ziaullah Langove escaped unharmed after armed attackers targeted his convoy in Mastung district on Friday, injuring six people, including three police personnel.The attack took place in the Khad Kocha area as Langove was travelling from Quetta to Kalat, Balochistan government spokesperson Shahid Rind said."Six people were injured in the attack, but the minister remained unhurt and the convoy has returned to Quetta," Rind said.All six injured people suffered bullet wounds, according to a senior police official. Three of them were police personnel, with two reportedly in serious condition. They were taken to a hospital in Quetta for treatment.The attack has raised fresh security concerns in Khad Kocha, an area that has repeatedly come under attack in recent weeks.According to officials, this was the fourth attack on travellers along the same highway since last month. Insurgents have repeatedly targeted people travelling through the area despite a major security operation carried out following the earlier incidents.Security forces have now sealed off the area and launched a search operation to locate those responsible for the latest attack.The incident adds to the continuing security challenges in Balochistan, where armed insurgent groups have carried out attacks against security forces and civilians.
Article Summary: Balochistan home minister Mir Ziaullah Langove escaped unharmed after armed attackers targeted his convoy. The attack took place in the Khad Kocha area as Langove was travelling from Quetta to Kalat. All six injured people suffered bullet wounds, according to a senior police official.

Article Title: 'Water is our red line': Shehbaz Sharif threatens India with 'direct response' over Indus Treaty
Article Text:
Shehbaz Sharif speaking on eve of Pakistan's Independence Day

Poll Vote & Share your view Should the Indus Waters Treaty be renegotiated? Yes, it needs changes No, it should remain unchanged 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Pakistan has yet again raked up India’s suspension of the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT), with its Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif threatening a “direct response” to New Delhi’s move, which came days after the Pahalgam terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir in April last year."The Prime Minister said that India has proven itself an enemy of peace by unilaterally and illegally suspending the Indus Waters Treaty. He announced that every drop of Pakistan's water is our red line. There will be no compromise on the water issue. If India does not come to the right path, we will give it a direct response," the Pakistan Prime Minister's Office said in a statement on X.Sharif, speaking at an event on the eve of Pakistan’s Independence Day (August 14), sought to portray India as an “enemy of peace” over New Delhi’s decision to keep the IWT in abeyance following the April 22 Pahalgam terror attack, in which 26 civilians were killed.He said New Delhi had proved itself an “enemy” of peace by putting the treaty in abeyance."India proved itself an enemy of peace by unilaterally and illegally suspending the Indus Waters Treaty. I declare in clear terms that every single drop of Pakistan's water is our red line. If India does not come to its senses, it will be responded to directly," the Pakistani premier added.The military hostilities ended on May 10 after Islamabad sought a ceasefire following India’s air strikes on multiple Pakistani air bases.The conflict erupted after India's Operation Sindoor in retaliation for the Pahalgam attack.New Delhi kept the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance after a Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS) meeting on April 23, 2025, and asserted that the conditions under which the treaty was negotiated have "fundamentally changed."India has asserted the treaty can no longer function in its present form and will remain in abeyance until Pakistan “credibly and irrevocably” ends its support for cross-border terrorism.The Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) was signed in September 1960.
Article Summary: Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif threatens a "direct response" to India's suspension of the Indus Waters Treaty. The move came days after the Pahalgam terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir in April last year. New Delhi kept the IWT in abeyance after a Cabinet Committee on Security meeting on April 23, 2025.

Article Title: Why US is questioning Pakistan's Rs 3 trillion defence spending
Article Text:
The US also criticised Islamabad for not publishing its executive budget proposal within a reasonable period (representative image)

US asks Pakistan to improve defence and debt transparency

Pakistan's defence allocation rises to Rs 3 trillion

Defence spending remains a key transparency concern

The US state department has flagged a lack of adequate parliamentary and civilian oversight of Pakistan's military and intelligence spending, while also raising concerns over limited disclosure of government debt and delays in publishing the executive budget proposal.The concerns were highlighted in the 2026 Fiscal Transparency Report, which assessed Pakistan's public financial transparency and identified gaps in the country's budgetary and fiscal disclosure practices.The report noted that Pakistan made its enacted budget and end-of-year financial statements widely available online. However, it said military and intelligence budgets remained outside adequate parliamentary or civilian public scrutiny.“The military and intelligence budgets were not subject to adequate parliamentary or civilian public oversight,” the report said.The US also criticised Islamabad for not publishing its executive budget proposal within a reasonable period.According to the assessment, this limits the time available for lawmakers and civil society to examine government spending before the budget is adopted.The state department called for three key changes to Pakistan's fiscal transparency framework.It urged Islamabad to make its executive budget proposal publicly available within a reasonable period, disclose detailed information about government debt obligations, including liabilities linked to state-owned enterprises, and bring military and intelligence agency budgets under parliamentary or civilian public oversight.The report also raised concerns about Pakistan's disclosure of public debt, saying only limited information was available on debt obligations, including those of major state-owned enterprises.At the same time, the US assessment acknowledged some positive aspects of Pakistan's public financial system.It said the country's supreme audit institution met international standards of independence and noted that its audit reports were published in a timely manner and contained substantive findings.The US assessment comes against the backdrop of a substantial increase in Pakistan's defence allocation for the 2026-27 financial year.In June, Pakistan's federal government proposed allocating Rs 3 trillion for defence services, up 17.65 per cent from the previous year's initial allocation of Rs 2.55 trillion, according to Dawn.The proposed defence services allocation amounts to about 2.08 per cent of Pakistan's projected GDP of Rs 143.6 trillion and nearly 16 per cent of the federal government's total outlay of Rs 18.77 trillion.Spending on civil works related to military infrastructure was projected to rise 7.92 per cent to Rs 363.16 billion, from Rs 336.49 billion previously.Military pensions are accounted for separately from the main defence services budget. The government has allocated Rs 822 billion for retired military personnel under the federal pension outlay, according to Dawn.The allocation for defence administration was set at Rs 10.9 billion, compared with Rs 7.9 billion in the outgoing fiscal year's original budget. That allocation was later revised to Rs 11.75 billion.Major military imports and defence acquisitions are generally funded outside the main defence services allocation and remain undisclosed.The US state department's assessment therefore highlights a distinction between Pakistan's publicly disclosed defence allocation and the wider military spending that may not be fully visible through the country's budgetary documents.The state department's recommendations focus on bringing military and intelligence expenditure into the broader framework of public financial oversight.While the report recognised that Pakistan publishes key budget documents, it identified defence and intelligence spending, debt disclosure and the timing of budget publication as areas requiring greater transparency.The recommendations would require Pakistan to give lawmakers and the public greater visibility into military and intelligence allocations, as well as government liabilities linked to state-owned enterprises.
Article Summary: US asks Pakistan to improve defence and debt transparency. Pakistan's defence allocation rises to Rs 3 trillion for 2026-27 financial year. US state department flagged a lack of adequate parliamentary and civilian oversight of Pakistan's military and intelligence spending. Report also raised concerns over limited disclosure of government debt and delays in publishing executive budget proposal.

Article Title: PML-N set to form 'government' in PoK after two former 'premiers' lose strongholds in third phase
Article Text:
Two former PoK premiers lost their strongholds in the third phase of elections marred by violence and rigging allegations, as the PML-N emerged dominant

Two former so-called prime ministers of Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) lost their traditional strongholds in the third phase of elections, according to unofficial results released on Tuesday, while incumbent premier Faisal Mumtaz Rathore of the Pakistan People's Party (PPP) retained his seat.The latest results came after voting in four constituencies on Monday, with the election process again overshadowed by violence and allegations of rigging. Polling in the remaining seven constituencies was postponed over concerns about the law-and-order situation and is expected to be held on August 21, according to the region's election commission.The PPP won two of the four seats contested in the third phase, while the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and the Awami Dast-o-Bazu Party won one each. The latter is backed by both Jamaat-e-Islami and Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).Former prime minister and Muslim Conference president Sardar Attique Ahmed Khan, who was backed by the PML-N, lost the seat in Western Bagh's Dhirkot constituency to Awami Dast-o-Bazu Party candidate Sardar Sajid Iqbal, according to unofficial results. The seat had been held by the Muslim Conference/PML-N since 1985.In Central Bagh, PPP's Zia Qamar retained the seat, defeating PML-N candidate Mushtaq Minhas.Former premier Sardar Tanveer Ilyas, who joined the Istehkam-i-Pakistan Party, secured only a few thousand votes.The result in Eastern Bagh remained pending after authorities ordered a re-poll at 12 polling stations. PML-N candidate Sardar Mir Akbar was leading based on results from 174 of the constituency's 186 polling stations, followed by PPP candidate Sardar Qamaruz Zaman Khan.The election comes against the backdrop of a striking shift in the Pakistani government's treatment of the protest movement that has rocked PoK for months.Just days before the final phase of voting, Pakistan's defence minister Khawaja Asif had described the protesters as "enemies of Pakistan" and ruled out talks with them. But Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's adviser Rana Sanaullah subsequently said 99% of those associated with the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) were "patriotic brothers", promising that a PML-N government would engage with the group and seek to resolve its demands.The reversal in rhetoric came as the PML-N emerged as the dominant force in the election and prepared to form the next government in the region. The party has secured 25 of the 45 directly elected seats so far, while the PPP has won 12 and the Awami Dast-o-Bazu Party one.The first two phases, held on July 27 and August 2, were also marked by violent protests and allegations of widespread rigging, with the PML-N and PPP accusing each other of electoral malpractice. Supporters of the two parties clashed at several polling stations.The JAAC has been protesting across the region since early June, with demands including the abolition of 12 refugee seats that it says can be used to influence the formation of governments in PoK.The group has alleged that more than 40 people were killed during violence surrounding the first phase of voting and that around 400 protesters had been killed since the protests began. The Pakistani government has rejected the higher figure as exaggerated, while Sanaullah has acknowledged that deaths from the unrest were in the "double figures".India does not recognise Pakistan's control over the territory, maintaining that Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh are integral and inalienable parts of India and describing Pakistan's presence in areas under its control as "illegal and forcible occupation".
Article Summary: Two former so-called prime ministers of Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) lost their traditional strongholds in the third phase of elections. Incumbent premier Faisal Mumtaz Rathore of the Pakistan People's Party (PPP) retained his seat. Polling in the remaining seven constituencies was postponed over concerns about the law-and-order situation.

Article Title: 'Discontent answered with bullets': MEA slams Pakistan over PoK crackdown
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Tuesday slammed Pakistan for its ongoing crackdown on protesters in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, calling upon the international community to hold the country accountable for the "gross violation of human rights. "During the bi-weekly press briefing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said that public discontent in PoK was answered with bullets and blackouts by authorities in Pakistan."We would like to highlight the human rights violations being committed in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir and other parts of the country. We call upon the international community to hold Pakistan accountable for its misdeeds, abuses and gross violations of human rights, including against its own people," Jaiswal said."Over the last several months, we have seen large-scale protests in PoK, including during and before the elections. Public discontent was answered with bullets, blackouts, repression and oppression. More than 90 people have been killed and many more injured. This has made news across the world," he added.Also Read | 'Arunachal is integral part of India, nothing can change this': MEA on China's fresh 'objections' The remarks came as at least 90 people, including protesters, security personnel and bystanders, were killed in clashes during June and July.The banned Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) has been staging protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) since June over the contentious 12 refugee seats. It has alleged that Pakistan's establishment manipulates these seats to install a prime minister of its choice to lead the so-called PoK government.Meanwhile, the third phase of elections in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) was held on Monday in four constituencies, amid violence and allegations of rigging. Polling started in Poonch Division’s Bagh and Haveli districts at 8 am, while elections in seven constituencies have been indefinitely postponed.Clashes between Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) and Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) workers were reported in some areas as the region's election commission classified most of the 803 polling stations as "sensitive or highly sensitive".After the first and second phases of polling, which were marred by violent protests and were held on July 27 and August 2, respectively, voting was scheduled for Monday in 11 constituencies of the Poonch Division in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir. There are 53 seats in the so-called PoK Legislative Assembly - 45 are directly elected, while eight are reserved for women, technocrats and clerics.The second phase of polling on August 2 was marred by violence and allegations of rigging. One person was killed and several others were injured.Also read | British national killed in PoK clashes; another held for over 2 months, says report The phase also included voting for the 12 refugee seats, which are at the centre of the ongoing controversy.Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) swept the second phase, winning 16 seats, while Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) secured the remaining five. In the first phase on July 27, PML-N won nine of the 13 seats, while PPP won four. With the first two phases combined, PML-N has already secured 24 seats.
Article Summary: MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said that public discontent in PoK was answered with bullets and blackouts by authorities in Pakistan. At least 90 people, including protesters, security personnel and bystanders, were killed in clashes during June and July. The banned Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) has been staging protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) since June.

Article Title: After weeks of violent protests, PoK votes in final election phase amid PTI, JAAC boycott calls
Article Text:
Pakistan’s elections were marked by protests and violence, raising concerns over security, political stability and the credibility of the electoral process.

Polling for Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir's so called assembly elections entered its final phase on Monday amid heightened security and reports of Islamabad-backed crackdown in the region.Voting is being held despite boycott calls from the Imran Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf's (PTI) PoJK unit and the Pakistan-banned Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC).The tussle between the JAAC and the Shehbaz Sharif-Asim Munir duo's crackdown has made the situation grim in PoK.India has also strongly condemned the crackdown on protesters. The MEA has called the so-called assembly elections in the illegally occupied region as a "farce".The MEA also condemned Pakistan's actions that led to the killing of 90 civilians in PoK.Meanwhile, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf’s (PTI) PoJK unit has announced a complete boycott of the ongoing electoral process in Pakistan-occupied Jammu & Kashmir (PoJK), calling it “unconstitutional” and “unfair”.The election has taken place against the backdrop of weeks of protests led by the JAAC, which has been demanding greater political rights for residents of Pakistan-occupied Kashmir.The final phase also came after media curbs, and other major restrictions imposed by Islamabad authority.The demonstrations have also seen clashes with security forces, overshadowing the election campaign.The ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) has already secured a majority in the assembly, seeing a likely return after a decade.
Article Summary: Polling for Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir's so called assembly elections entered its final phase on Monday. Voting is being held despite boycott calls from the Imran Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf's (PTI) PoJK unit and the Pakistan-banned Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) The election has taken place against the backdrop of weeks of protests.

Article Title: LeT man dies in Pakistan after meal, speculation of poisoning
Article Text:
Qari Saeed Abdul Aziz had played a key role in the planning of many terror strikes, including the 26/11 Mumbai attack

LeT operative was involved in the 26/11 Mumbai attack
