Article Title: From 'enemies' to 'patriotic brothers': Pakistan changes stance on PoK protesters ahead of polls
Article Text:
Pakistan PML-N has softened its stance on PoK protesters, calling them "patriotic brothers", as the party prepares to form a government in the region.

Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif ’s led PML-N appears to be softening its position towards protesters in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK), with a senior government adviser now describing the vast majority of demonstrators as “patriotic” and saying the party will soon engage with them.Sharif’s adviser Rana Sanaullah on Saturday said 99 per cent of those associated with the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), the group leading months of protests in the region, were “our patriotic brothers”.“When the PML(N) government will be formed with two-third majority, it will sit with [Joint Awami] Action Committee representatives. Their first task will be to resolve this issue,” Sanaullah said at a rally ahead of the third and final phase of elections in PoK.The remarks mark a notable shift from the government's earlier rhetoric towards the protesters.Just days earlier, Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif had likened the protesters to India and described them as “enemies of Pakistan”, ruling out talks with them. Asif had said there would be “no dialogue with the protesters” and that he considered them in the same category as India.India, however, has rejected Pakistan's stance on the unrest, saying the protests are a direct consequence of Pakistan's economic exploitation, denial of fundamental rights and administrative oppression in PoK.Sanaullah had also previously accused the protesters of seeking to seize Muzaffarabad and Mirpur by force and described their actions as an “India-like attack”. The government had disputed claims of civilian deaths during clashes and accused protesters of opening fire at security personnel.The JAAC, however, has alleged that security forces opened fire on its activists during protests and long marches, with the group claiming that more than 40 people, including women and children, had been killed since elections began and around 400 protesters had been killed since early June.The Pakistan government has rejected the JAAC's figures as “overly exaggerated”, though Sanaullah has acknowledged that the number of people killed in the protests was in the “two digits” and that security personnel had also died.The change in tone comes as the PML-N prepares to take charge of the so-called government in PoK following elections that have been accompanied by violence and allegations of rigging.In the first two phases of voting, the PML-N has won 25 of the 45 directly elected seats, crossing the majority mark in the so-called legislative assembly. The party is in a direct contest with the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP), its coalition partner in Pakistan's federal government.The third and final phase of polling for four seats is scheduled for Monday, while elections in seven constituencies have been indefinitely postponed.The JAAC has been leading protests in PoK since June, drawing support from students, traders, transporters, lawyers and social workers. The regional government banned the group in June.The protests have faced a security crackdown, with Amnesty International and the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan raising concerns over reports of violence and calling for investigations.The situation also drew concern from the United Nations, when it called for accountability for actions against people engaged in peaceful protest.The United States has also urged Pakistan to exercise restraint amid the unrest, calling on authorities to respect fundamental freedoms and create conditions for free and fair elections.
Article Summary: Pakistan PML-N appears to be softening its position towards protesters in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) A senior government adviser has now described the vast majority of demonstrators as “patriotic” The remarks mark a notable shift from the government's earlier rhetoric towards the protesters.

Article Title: 'Shouldn't be exclusive club': Pak minister seeks Nato-like Islamic military alliance
Article Text:
"I put the protesters of PojK in the same category as India and consider them as enemies," Khawaja Asif said.

A day after Pakistan signed a defence agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkey, Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif on Saturday called for Islamic countries to set aside their differences and form a military alliance along the lines of Nato.In an interview with Geo News, Asif said the agreement signed in Mecca should not remain an "exclusive club" and should be expanded to include other Islamic countries."See, we can't close the doors for other countries. This shouldn't be an exclusive club. This is my personal opinion. It should expand," Asif said."I think Muslim countries should keep their differences, transactional or bilateral disputes aside, on the lines of Nato and stand together," he added.Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey signed the defence pact in Mecca on Friday, marking a significant strategic development in the region. The agreement reportedly commits the three countries to regard an armed attack against any one of them as an attack against all three, drawing comparisons with Nato's Article 5 collective-defence principle.The pact brings together Saudi Arabia's financial strength, Turkey's defence industry and Nato experience, and Pakistan's large military and nuclear capabilities.According to Pakistan's foreign ministry, the agreement is "guided by the longstanding historical ties among the three states" and their shared strategic interests, defence cooperation and "enduring bonds of brotherhood and Islamic solidarity".The agreement aims to strengthen collective deterrence against aggression and stipulates that an armed attack against any of the three countries would be regarded as an attack against all, according to a joint statement.The pact comes as Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries face missile attacks and disruptions to energy shipments amid the ongoing conflict involving Iran and its regional allies. The conflict escalated after the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran on February 28, triggering a wider regional crisis.A Turkish official said the agreement was purely defensive, was not directed at any particular country and remained open to participation by other regional nations. The official added that it would not replace existing bilateral or multilateral security arrangements.
Article Summary: Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey signed the defence pact in Mecca on Friday. The agreement reportedly commits the three countries to regard an armed attack against any one of them as an attack against all three. The pact brings together Saudi Arabia's financial strength, Turkey's defence industry and Nato experience, and Pakistan's large military and nuclear capabilities.

Article Title: Sheikh Hasina says she will return to Bangladesh in December. What awaits her back home
Article Text:
Sheikh Hasina has been living in India since her government was toppled on August 5, 2024

Shekh Hasina's road back to Bangladesh

Shekh Hasina's trial was held in-absentia as she is in India

A return plan and a high-stakes gamble

Sheikh Hasina: A factfile

Politics behind Sheikh Hasina’s Bangladesh return plan

Sheikh Hasina return: What could unfold in Bangladesh

Banned and bruised: What happens to Awami League

Inside Sheikh Hasina's family

What lies ahead for Sheikh Hasina

For the first time since fleeing Bangladesh two years ago, Sheikh Hasina has put a specific month on her planned return: December.In July, nearly a month before the second anniversary of the fall of her government, the 78-year-old former prime minister said she intended to return to Bangladesh in December along with senior Awami League leaders and surrender to the courts.On August 5, the second anniversary of the collapse of her government, Hasina repeated that pledge despite the enormous legal and political risks involved.She has already been sentenced to death in absentia over crimes against humanity linked to her administration’s crackdown on the July 2024 uprising, in which up to 1,400 people were killed, according to UN estimates. Hasina has rejected the charges and has described the proceedings against her as "politically motivated."The question now is not simply whether she will follow through on her return plan. It is what she hopes to achieve by announcing it and what awaits her if she goes back.Hasina’s announcement is striking because the risks of returning are unusually high.She herself has acknowledged that she could be arrested or even killed.“They (Bangladesh government) may arrest me on my return, they may even kill me. Still, I have to go.If death comes, I want it to come on my own soil, where my parents are buried and where their blood was shed,” the former prime minister said on August 5, referring to the 1975 assassination of her parents and three of her four siblings by a group of army officers.Her December plan therefore leaves her facing difficult choices.If she returns, she could be taken into custody almost immediately and remain out of active politics for an extended period. If she stays in India, meanwhile, she remains vulnerable to accusations from opponents that she is unwilling to face the legal process at home.By naming December, however, Hasina has also put a clear timeline on her own political future and brought the question of her return back into Bangladesh’s political debate.Whether or not she ultimately follows through, the announcement keeps attention on both her and the Awami League at a time when the party has little room to operate politically.The Awami League’s activities were first banned under the Muhammad Yunus-led interim administration in 2025, and the restrictions were subsequently given legal backing by parliament in 2026.Through her remarks from India, Hasina has continued to present herself both as a prime minister whose government was toppled and as a victim of what she describes as a foreign-backed conspiracy.Her August 5 address, at a virtual press conference in New Delhi, followed a similar pattern. She criticised Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s government and called for the ban on the Awami League to be lifted.Her proposed return also has obvious implications for the party.It gives Awami League supporters a rallying point and keeps Hasina at the centre of discussions about the party’s future, despite the legal risks she faces if she goes back.A political leader can remain influential even without holding office, particularly when supporters continue to identify strongly with that leader and believe the political system has treated the party unfairly.Hasina’s announcement, therefore, serves another purpose: it prevents her from disappearing from the political conversation while the Awami League remains barred from normal political activity.Hasina has made a dramatic return from exile once before.In 1981, after nearly six years abroad following the assassination of most of her family, she returned to Bangladesh from India as the newly elected president of the Awami League.Then, large crowds gathered to welcome her.This time, the circumstances could hardly be more different.Anti-Hasina sentiment remains strong, even though her father, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, occupies a central place in Bangladesh’s independence history.Hostility towards the Awami League has also extended beyond the former prime minister herself.For instance, the family home of Shakib Al Hasan, one of Bangladesh’s most celebrated cricketers and a former Awami League MP, was targeted with petrol bombs just hours after his virtual appearance in the August 5 media interaction.Awami League leaders themselves acknowledge the possibility of violence if senior figures, particularly Hasina, return.“We will have to face whatever happens... There will be a backlash because the extremists are highly weaponised. We are preparing for this,” senior party leader Mohibul Chowdhury said a day after Hasina announced her return plan.On its part, the incumbent government led by Tarique Rahman, son of Hasina’s longtime political rival Khaleda Zia, has little obvious political incentive to make her return easy.The Awami League government was removed after a mass uprising, and the political order that followed has been built partly around a rejection of Hasina’s rule.The Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) government has already indicated that she would be arrested if she returns.Her arrival could therefore become an immediate test of how the government handles both the legal process against her and the political consequences that could follow.Although Sheikh Mujibur Rahman was among the Awami League’s co-founders, the party gradually became synonymous with Sheikh Hasina, who has been its undisputed leader for more than four decades.Her political future is therefore tied to another question: can the party survive without her?The Awami League’s organisational strength was heavily dependent on Hasina’s leadership. Since her departure, with several senior leaders also in exile, underground or in custody, no obvious figure has emerged who appears capable of filling the political space she left behind.Her children do not offer an obvious alternative either.Her son, Sajeeb Wazed Joy, a dual US-Bangladeshi citizen, was previously involved with the Awami League and served as an adviser to his mother, but has not emerged as her political successor. Her daughter, Saima Wazed, meanwhile, has remained away from politics and is a senior World Health Organization official.That makes Hasina’s continued political activity important for the Awami League.Her return pledge gives supporters something to rally around at a time when the party remains politically marginalised.But it also creates a dilemma.A comeback centred entirely on Sheikh Hasina could keep the Awami League’s identity alive, but it could also make it harder for the party to develop new leadership and a new political message.The environment that sustained Hasina for years has changed sharply. Public resentment towards her remains strong, while the legal cases and allegations of abuses against her government have made any political comeback far more difficult.Since late 2024, Dhaka has been seeking Hasina’s extradition from India, while New Delhi has said the requests are being examined under established legal processes.Bangladesh has also linked progress on her extradition to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s proposed maiden official visit to India.A voluntary return by Hasina could remove one of the most contentious issues in India-Bangladesh relations, although it would not by itself resolve the wider strains between the two governments.Whether she actually follows through on her December pledge remains uncertain.If she does return, the immediate risks are clear: arrest, incarceration and possibly, the enforcement of a death sentence handed down in absentia.Her presence could also reignite political tensions in a deeply divided country.At the same time, returning would give Hasina something she currently lacks from exile — a chance to physically reconnect with supporters and place herself once again at the centre of Bangladesh’s political drama.December, therefore, could become a defining moment for Sheikh Hasina. It could mark the beginning of a comeback or the end of her career as an active political force.
Article Summary: Sheikh Hasina has been living in India since her government was toppled on August 5, 2024. In July, nearly a month before the second anniversary of the fall of her government, the 78-year-old former prime minister said she intended to return to Bangladesh in December. She has already been sentenced to death over crimes against humanity.

Article Title: Nepal Speaker orders PM Balen to face House on Aug 26; attended just 5 of 39 sittings
Article Text:
Opposition parties had been demanding Shah's presence since May, accusing him of avoiding parliamentary scrutiny. Lawmakers have also questioned his continued absence during a debate on communal unrest in Sunsari.

Nepal Speaker Dol Prasad Aryal has ordered PM Balendra Shah to appear before the country's House of Representatives on Aug 26 and answer lawmakers directly, issuing a rare parliamentary rebuke to a PM who attended just five of the first 39 sittings since taking office and faced months of opposition protests over his absence and controversial remarks on the India-Nepal border.Aryal issued the directive after repeated demands from opposition lawmakers for Shah to face Parliament. “I rule that the right honourable prime minister attend the meeting of the House of Representatives and answer questions from honourable members,” he said. The ruling ended a 77-day opposition protest over Shah's failure to clarify his border remarks. Under House rules, the first hour of one sitting in the first week of every month is reserved for lawmakers to directly question the PM.Opposition parties had been demanding Shah's presence since May, accusing him of avoiding parliamentary scrutiny. Lawmakers have also questioned his continued absence during a debate on communal unrest in Sunsari, where four people were killed, in the last week of July.Nepali Congress whip Nischal Rai had warned that opposition protests would continue unless Shah appeared before the House. “Has the PM escaped questions and tried to weaken democracy?” Rai asked, adding, “If the prime minister remains absent, the protest will continue.”Shah's May 31 appearance triggered a bigger confrontation. Responding to a question on Nepal's border dispute with India, Shah said, “After becoming PM, I came to know that not only has India encroached on Nepal’s land, but Nepal has also encroached on India’s land.” He added: “Both sides need to sit down and look into the matter.”Opposition parties demanded evidence, withdrawal of the statement and an apology, arguing that it weakened Nepal's position on Kalapani, Lipulekh and Limpiyadhura. Shram Sanskriti Party lawmaker Harka Rai rejected a subsequent clarification by foreign minister Shishir Khanal, saying the person who made the mistake “must come and rectify it”. Khanal had told the House that Shah was referring to cross-border occupation and encroachment in no-man's-land areas rather than a formal Nepalese territorial claim over Indian land.
Article Summary: Nepal Speaker Dol Prasad Aryal has ordered PM Balendra Shah to appear before the country's House of Representatives on Aug 26. Opposition parties had been demanding Shah's presence since May, accusing him of avoiding parliamentary scrutiny. Lawmakers have also questioned his continued absence during a debate on communal unrest in Sunsari.

Article Title: Nepal: Break Agniveer hiring deadlock, Gorkha veterans press Balen government
Article Text:

Calls for Nepal to allow its citizens to join the Indian Army under its Agnipath scheme have grown louder ahead of Army chief General Dhiraj Seth's scheduled participation in an ex-servicemen rally for Gorkha veterans in Pokhara Wednesday, bringing the stalled recruitment issue back into focus during his three-day visit.Days before Gen Seth's arrival, hundreds of former Indian Army personnel, their families, and Gorkha aspirants marched in Pokhara, urging Nepal PM Balen Shah to allow recruitment under Agnipath. They submitted a memorandum to Shah and home minister Sudan Gurung.The deadlock has remained an unresolved backdrop to Gen Seth's visit, though official accounts of his talks with Nepal Army chief General Ashok Raj Sigdel have made no mention of the issue. Gen Seth was conferred the honorary rank of General of the Nepal Army by President Ramchandra Paudel Monday. Gen Seth met Shah in Kathmandu Tuesday, but Agnipath found no public mention in the official statement.Colonel Krishna Bahadur Khatri (retd) told TOI from Kathmandu that Nepal's stand had "deprived its youths of an opportunity still seen by many Gorkha families as far better than low-paid employment overseas".Captain Rudra Thapa (retd) said the freeze had pushed many young men towards low-paid, physically demanding jobs in the Gulf and other countries when they could have earned a far income through military service. "If they were allowed to join Indian Army as Agniveers, they could have earned around Nepalese Rs 45-50 lakh, including benefits, in four years," Thapa said."If govt does not allow recruitment into foreign armies, it must be able to provide employment at home."India introduced Agnipath in June 2022, under which recruits serve for four years and up to 25% may later be absorbed into regular service. Nepal declined to allow recruitment under the new terms, arguing that the four-year contractual model marked a departure from the long-term service and pension arrangement that underpinned the 1947 tripartite agreement. No Nepal-domiciled Gorkhas have been recruited since.
Article Summary: Nepal refuses to allow its citizens to join the Indian Army under its Agnipath scheme. Army chief General Dhiraj Seth scheduled to participate in an ex- servicemen rally for Gorkha veterans in Pokhara Wednesday. Hundreds of former Indian Army personnel, their families, and Gorkha aspirants urged Nepal PM Balen Shah to allow recruitment.
